answer:
Seven German drivers born 1971–1985 are in the data. The query returns all seven, sorted by Q3 count (descending), with ties broken by older date of birth first. Two drivers have zero Q3 times and are still listed.

| Forename | Surname | Wikipedia link | Date of birth | Q3 times |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nico | Rosberg | http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nico_Rosberg | 1985-06-27 | 149 |
| Nick | Heidfeld | http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Heidfeld | 1977-05-10 | 44 |
| Adrian | Sutil | http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Sutil | 1983-01-11 | 19 |
| Ralf | Schumacher | http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralf_Schumacher | 1975-06-30 | 15 |
| Timo | Glock | http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timo_Glock | 1982-03-18 | 13 |
| Markus | Winkelhock | http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markus_Winkelhock | 1980-06-13 | 0 |
| André | Lotterer | http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Lotterer | 1981-11-19 | 0 |

Readings I chose:
- "German" means nationality exactly `'German'`. The data also has `'East German'` as a separate value, which I left out.
- A Q3 time is a `qualifying.q3` value that is neither NULL nor empty, following the wiki's convention.
- "Entire career" means every qualifying row in the database, with no season filter.
- The Wikipedia link is `drivers.url`, and the date of birth is `drivers.dob`.
- Drivers with no Q3 time are kept with a count of 0, since the question asks for every German driver in the range.

The query was run against `db.sqlite` read-only and returned the seven rows above.

sql: SELECT c.nationality, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN r.rank = 1 THEN c.constructorId END) AS constructor_count FROM constructors AS c LEFT JOIN results AS r ON r.constructorId = c.constructorId GROUP BY c.nationality ORDER BY c.nationality
answer: Counted each constructor once per nationality if it has at least one race result with results.rank = 1 (the official Fastest Lap Rank). All 24 nationalities in the constructors table are listed. Nationalities with at least one such constructor: British 4; German 2; Italian 2; Austrian, French, Indian, Japanese, Swiss 1 each. The other 15 nationalities show 0. The constructors and results Terms are draft, not certified. The query ran successfully and returned 24 rows.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS unstated_transactions FROM trans AS t WHERE (t.k_symbol IS NULL OR TRIM(t.k_symbol) = '') AND t.account_id IN (SELECT d.account_id FROM disp AS d JOIN client AS c ON c.client_id = d.client_id WHERE d.type = 'OWNER' AND c.gender = 'M' AND STRFTIME('%Y', c.birth_date) IN ('1974', '1975', '1976'))
answer:
17195

Interpretation I used:
- "Accounts held by" means the account's OWNER disposition (disp.type = 'OWNER'), not any authorized user (DISPONENT). Each account has exactly one owner, so the owner link does not multiply rows.
- "No payment purpose noted" means trans.k_symbol is NULL or blank (TRIM(k_symbol) = ''). Those are the same rows as the ontology's "No Characterization Recorded" filter.
- "Whole recorded history" means no date filter.
- Male customers born 1974 to 1976 means client.gender = 'M' and the birth year from client.birth_date is 1974, 1975 or 1976.

The query ran without errors and returned 17195 rows as a single count. The Terms it relies on (Client, Disposition, Transaction) are still draft, not certified. I have not saved this as a verified example because you haven't confirmed it yet.

sql: WITH owner_male AS (SELECT DISTINCT x.account_id FROM disp AS x JOIN client AS c ON c.client_id = x.client_id WHERE x.type = 'OWNER' AND c.gender = 'M'), yearly AS (SELECT STRFTIME('%Y', l.date) AS y, SUM(l.amount) AS total FROM loan AS l JOIN owner_male AS o ON o.account_id = l.account_id WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', l.date) IN ('1996', '1997') GROUP BY y) SELECT 100.0 * (SUM(CASE WHEN y = '1997' THEN total END) - SUM(CASE WHEN y = '1996' THEN total END)) / SUM(CASE WHEN y = '1996' THEN total END) AS pct_growth FROM yearly;

The percentage growth in total loan amount from 1996 to 1997 for loans on accounts owned by male clients is about 25.30% (25.3001912227906 unrounded). Total approved amount was 10,084,572 in 1996 (59 loans) and 12,635,988 in 1997 (94 loans).

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.ID) FROM Patient AS p WHERE p.Description IS NULL AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND ((l.CRP GLOB '[0-9]*' AND CAST(l.CRP AS REAL) >= 1.0) OR (l.CRP LIKE '%+%' AND l.CRP <> '+-') OR l.CRP LIKE '>%'))
answer:
42 patients. The query counts distinct patients whose Patient.Description is NULL and who have at least one Laboratory row with a positive CRP.

Interpretation choices:
- CRP is stored as text. The docs give the normal range as "N = -, +-, or N < 1.0", so I treated a result as positive when it is a number ≥ 1.0 (e.g., "1", "2.5"), contains "+" (e.g., "+", "2+", "6+<") other than the "+-" normal value, or starts with ">" (e.g., ">6", ">7.0").
- Results "-", "<x" values, "0.xx" numbers, and "+-" count as negative.
- "M" (1 row) is not clearly positive or negative in the docs, so I excluded it. Including it would not change the count unless that patient qualifies on another row.
- "No recorded patient description" means Description IS NULL. The docs say null or empty means not recorded; there are no empty strings in the data, so NULL is the only case.
- All Laboratory IDs match a Patient row, so no lab rows are lost by the join.

The query ran against db.sqlite and returned 42.

sql: WITH rare AS (SELECT element FROM atom GROUP BY element HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT molecule_id) = 1) SELECT m.molecule_id, COUNT(DISTINCT c.bond_id) AS bond_count FROM molecule AS m JOIN atom AS a ON a.molecule_id = m.molecule_id AND a.element IN (SELECT element FROM rare) LEFT JOIN connected AS c ON c.atom_id = a.atom_id WHERE m.label = '+' GROUP BY m.molecule_id ORDER BY m.molecule_id;
answer:
Result (3 rows):

| molecule_id | bond_count |
|---|---|
| TR238 | 0 |
| TR430 | 6 |
| TR499 | 1 |

How I read the question:
- "Rare" means the element appears in exactly one molecule across the whole `atom` table, regardless of label. That gives ca, cu, i, k, pb, y, zn. sn (2 molecules) is not rare.
- A qualifying molecule is one labelled '+' that contains at least one of these elements.
- The bond count is the number of distinct bonds that have at least one end on an atom of that rare element in that molecule. I used `connected`, which is symmetric, so each atom's bonds appear under its own `atom_id`.

Notes:
- TR238's zinc atom is isolated (no bonds), so it qualifies with a count of 0. I kept it rather than dropping it. An inner join to `connected` would remove it.
- No carcinogenic molecule contains two different rare elements, so one row per molecule is unambiguous.
- TR430 is the copper molecule (6 Cu–H bonds). TR499 is the yttrium molecule (one Y–P triple bond).
- I ran the query read-only and did not edit the wiki.

sql: WITH bud AS (SELECT b.link_to_event AS event_id, SUM(b.amount) AS budgeted FROM budget AS b GROUP BY b.link_to_event), exp AS (SELECT b.link_to_event AS event_id, SUM(x.cost) AS spent_exp FROM expense AS x JOIN budget AS b ON b.budget_id = x.link_to_budget GROUP BY b.link_to_event), ratios AS (SELECT e.event_name, CAST(COALESCE(exp.spent_exp, 0) AS REAL) / bud.budgeted AS ratio FROM event AS e INNER JOIN bud ON bud.event_id = e.event_id LEFT JOIN exp ON exp.event_id = e.event_id WHERE e.status = 'Closed') SELECT event_name FROM ratios WHERE ratio = (SELECT MAX(ratio) FROM ratios) ORDER BY event_name
answer:
Three closed events are tied for the highest ratio of total spending to total budget: 'Officers meeting - November', 'Officers meeting - October', and 'Officers meeting - September'. Each spent $20.20 against a $20 total budget, a ratio of 1.01.

Readings I chose:
- "Closed" means event.status = 'Closed' (18 events).
- "Total spending" is the sum of expense.cost per event. This matches the sum of budget.spent for every closed event, so the choice does not change the result.
- "Total budget amount" is the sum of budget.amount per event. Budget lines are summed per event before the join to expenses, so the expenses do not inflate the budget total.

The next highest ratio is 'September Speaker' at 1.0012 ($260.32 / $260), so the Officers meetings are clearly ahead. The query returned 3 rows, not truncated.

The Event, Budget and Expense Terms used here are draft, not certified.

sql: WITH t AS (SELECT d.surname AS surname, r.name AS race_name, CAST(SUBSTR(q.q2,1,INSTR(q.q2,':')-1) AS INTEGER)*60000 + CAST(REPLACE(SUBSTR(q.q2,INSTR(q.q2,':')+1),'.','') AS INTEGER) AS q2_ms FROM qualifying q JOIN races r ON r.raceId=q.raceId JOIN drivers d ON d.driverId=q.driverId WHERE r.year=2017 AND q.q2 GLOB '[0-9]:[0-9][0-9].[0-9][0-9][0-9]') SELECT surname, race_name FROM t WHERE q2_ms = (SELECT MIN(q2_ms) FROM t)
answer:
The fastest Q2 time of the 2017 season in the database is 1:04.316, set by Bottas at the Austrian Grand Prix. No other driver shares that time, so the query returns one row: surname Bottas, race Austrian Grand Prix.

Caveat: the database has qualifying data only for 2017 rounds 2 to 14 (Chinese to Singapore). The Australian Grand Prix (round 1) and rounds 15 to 20 are missing, so this is the fastest among the races on record, not the full season.

Reading I chose: "Q2 time" means the q2 column. I compared the times numerically (minutes and seconds converted to milliseconds) because the column is stored as text. The query returns the surname and race name, in the order the question asked for them.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS qualifying_schools FROM satscores AS t JOIN schools AS s ON s.CDSCode = t.cds WHERE t.rtype = 'S' AND s.MailCity = 'San Francisco' AND s.DOCType IN ('Unified School District','High School District','Elementary School District','County Office of Education (COE)') AND t.AvgScrRead IS NOT NULL AND t.AvgScrMath IS NOT NULL AND t.AvgScrWrite IS NOT NULL AND (t.AvgScrRead + t.AvgScrMath + t.AvgScrWrite) >= 1500;
answer:
The count is **3**. The qualifying schools are Lowell High (total 1825), Asawa (Ruth) SF School of the Arts (1671), and Independence High (1509).

Choices I made:
- **Total SAT** is the sum of AvgScrRead, AvgScrMath, and AvgScrWrite, since the database doesn't store a total. A school is excluded if any of the three averages is NULL.
- **School rows only**: I used `satscores.rtype = 'S'` so district-level rows are not counted.
- **Mailing city** is exactly `'San Francisco'`. Two variants exist ('San Francico' and 'San Francisco, CA'), but neither has a total of 1500 or more, so including them would not change the count.
- **Status**: the question didn't mention it, so Closed and Pending schools are included. None of the three qualifying schools is closed.
- **"Public"**: I treated it as the four district types you listed, which is how the wiki defines public school districts. The State Board of Education school San Francisco Flex Academy (total 1512) is excluded by this filter.

The query ran read-only against `db.sqlite` and returned 3.

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(n), 2) AS avg_pit_stops FROM (SELECT r.raceId, COUNT(ps.stop) AS n FROM races AS r JOIN pitStops AS ps ON ps.raceId = r.raceId WHERE r.year = 2017 AND r.year <> 2000 GROUP BY r.raceId);
answer:
The average is 37.92 pit stops per race.

Choices I made:
- "Not hosted in 2000" is always true for 2017 races, so the filter removes nothing. I kept it in the query anyway.
- The 2017 races in the data are 19 (rounds 2 to 20). Six of them (Malaysian onward) have no rows in pitStops. I read that as pit stop data not being recorded, not as zero stops, so I averaged over the 13 races that have pit stop records: 493 stops / 13 races = 37.92.
- Counting the six missing races as zero gives 493 / 19 = 25.95. If you want that reading, change the join to a LEFT JOIN over all 2017 races.
- Each pit stop row counts as one stop, using the (raceId, driverId, stop) primary key.

I ran the query against db.sqlite and it returned 37.92.

100.0. Every card with commander format and Legal status has hasContentWarning = 0. Of the 55,235 distinct cards with a commander Legal legality, all 55,235 lack a content warning. The 29 cards with a content warning are not commander-legal.

Interpretation: "cards" means distinct card rows (uuid), counted once even if several legality rows match. The query returns the raw value with no rounding, since the question did not ask for rounding. Nine commander-Legal legality rows have no matching row in `cards`, so they are excluded from the denominator. I did not check this against `docs/verified_queries.md`, which I only read partly.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS patient_count FROM Patient AS p WHERE p.Admission = '-' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND (l.HCT <= 29 OR l.HCT >= 52)) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND CAST(l.RNP AS REAL) > 16);
answer:
The answer is 2.

Readings I chose:
- "Registry patients followed at the outpatient clinic" means every row in Patient with Admission = '-' (outpatient), with no restriction on thrombosis events. Blank and '+(' admission codes are not counted as outpatients.
- "Non-normal hematocrit" means HCT <= 29 or HCT >= 52, since the normal range in the docs is 29 < N < 52 and both endpoints fall outside it. Using strict < 29 or > 52 gives the same count of 2.
- "Anti-ribonuclear protein above 16" means CAST(RNP AS REAL) > 16 (strictly above). Non-numeric values such as 'negative' cast to 0 and do not count.
- Each condition is checked with EXISTS over all lab dates, so the two findings can come from different test dates. NULL HCT and RNP values do not qualify.

The query ran against db.sqlite and returned 2.

sql: WITH min_weight AS (SELECT MIN(weight_kg) AS w FROM superhero WHERE weight_kg > 0) SELECT MAX(power_count) AS max_superpowers FROM (SELECT s.id, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT hp.power_id) FROM hero_power AS hp WHERE hp.hero_id = s.id) AS power_count FROM superhero AS s WHERE s.weight_kg = (SELECT w FROM min_weight))

18

The lightest recorded weight is 14 kg (weight_kg > 0 excludes the 0 and NULL placeholders). Only one hero weighs 14 kg, Jack-Jack (id 361), and the query returns the largest power count among the heroes at that weight, which is 18. I counted distinct power_id per hero, and hero_power has no duplicate pairs, so the result is the same either way. The query was run against db.sqlite (read-only) and returned 18.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT b.bond_id) AS hydrogen_bond_count FROM atom AS y JOIN bond AS b ON b.molecule_id = y.molecule_id JOIN connected AS c ON c.bond_id = b.bond_id JOIN atom AS a1 ON a1.atom_id = c.atom_id JOIN atom AS a2 ON a2.atom_id = c.atom_id2 WHERE y.element = 'y' AND (a1.element = 'h' OR a2.element = 'h');
answer: 2. The yttrium atom is TR499_1, in molecule TR499. That molecule has 3 bonds, and 2 of them (TR499_2_3 and TR499_2_4, both single bonds from phosphorus to hydrogen) have a hydrogen at one end. I counted distinct bonds, not connected rows, since each bond appears twice in `connected`. I included all bond types, since the question asks about every bond.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS ruling_count FROM rulings AS r JOIN cards AS c ON c.uuid = r.uuid WHERE c.name = 'Mishra''s Factory' AND r.date = (SELECT MAX(r2.date) FROM rulings AS r2 JOIN cards AS c2 ON c2.uuid = r2.uuid WHERE c2.name = 'Mishra''s Factory');

sql:
WITH acc AS (
  SELECT a.account_id, d.A2 AS district_name
  FROM account AS a JOIN district AS d ON d.district_id = a.district_id
  WHERE d.A3 = 'north Bohemia' AND a.date BETWEEN '1996-01-01' AND '1996-12-31'
), last_bal AS (
  SELECT account_id, balance FROM (
    SELECT t.account_id, t.balance,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY t.account_id ORDER BY t.date DESC, t.trans_id DESC) AS rn
    FROM trans AS t
    WHERE t.date <= '1996-12-31' AND t.account_id IN (SELECT account_id FROM acc)
  ) WHERE rn = 1
)
SELECT acc.district_name AS district_name, COUNT(*) AS accounts_opened, ROUND(AVG(lb.balance), 2) AS avg_end_1996_balance
FROM acc JOIN last_bal AS lb ON lb.account_id = acc.account_id
GROUP BY acc.district_name ORDER BY acc.district_name;
answer:
Region: 'north Bohemia' (Litomerice is district 37 in that region). The query returns the per-district table, ordered by name. It was run against db.sqlite and returned 10 rows:

Ceska Lipa 18 31357.06; Chomutov 18 29084.28; Decin 12 34289.08; Jablonec n. Nisou 15 26449.40; Liberec 21 36765.81; Litomerice 9 27278.67; Louny 15 28686.00; Most 12 31364.25; Teplice 15 35322.07; Usti nad Labem 12 35476.25.

The other two results are not in the query, because the output asks for one column set. I computed them with separate checks on the same 147 accounts:
- Region-wide average end-of-1996 balance (across accounts, not district means): 31809.19.
- Highest district average: Liberec, 36765.81. No tie.

Interpretation choices:
- "Opened in 1996" uses account.date from 1996-01-01 to 1996-12-31.
- The end-of-1996 balance is trans.balance of the account's latest transaction with date ≤ 1996-12-31, ties broken by the highest trans_id. Every one of the 147 accounts has at least one transaction by then, so no account is dropped.
- Region matching uses district.A3 = 'north Bohemia' exactly, as the wiki notes it is stored in lowercase.

sql: SELECT d.forename, d.surname FROM qualifying AS q JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = q.raceId JOIN circuits AS c ON c.circuitId = r.circuitId JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = q.driverId WHERE r.year = 2008 AND c.name = 'Marina Bay Street Circuit' AND q.q3 IS NOT NULL AND q.q3 <> '' ORDER BY q.q3 LIMIT 1;
answer: Felipe Massa set the fastest Q3 time at Marina Bay Street Circuit in 2008, 1:44.801, at the 2008 Singapore Grand Prix. The query returns his forename and surname. I checked the result against the qualifying rows for that race, and there is no tie.

sql: WITH qual AS (SELECT DISTINCT link_to_member AS mid FROM expense WHERE cost > 50), lines AS (SELECT DISTINCT e.link_to_member AS mid, e.link_to_budget AS bid FROM expense AS e JOIN qual AS q ON q.mid = e.link_to_member) SELECT m.first_name, m.last_name, ROUND(SUM(b.remaining), 2) AS total_remaining FROM lines AS l JOIN member AS m ON m.member_id = l.mid JOIN budget AS b ON b.budget_id = l.bid GROUP BY m.member_id, m.first_name, m.last_name ORDER BY total_remaining DESC, m.last_name ASC, m.first_name ASC
answer:
The query returns 3 members (the 3 who have at least one expense over $50, from 22 such expenses in total):

1. Phillip Cullen: 107.30
2. Sacha Harrison: 50.83
3. Elijah Allen: 16.35

Readings I chose:
- A member qualifies if any of their expenses costs more than $50.
- For each qualifying member, the total covers all of their expenses on record, not only the over-$50 ones. Each budget line is counted once per member, even if several of their expenses are charged to it.
- The total is the sum of `budget.remaining` across those lines, so overdrawn lines (negative remaining) reduce the total.

The data is clean for this: no NULL `remaining` values, `remaining` matches `amount - spent` on every row, and every expense links to a valid budget line and member. The query ran read-only and I did not edit the wiki.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS eligible_patient_count FROM Patient AS p WHERE p.Birthday > '1980-01-01' AND (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND (l.FG < 150 OR l.FG > 450)) OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND (TRIM(l.`U-PRO`) IN ('3', '4', '%%', '300', '>=300', '>=1000') OR TRIM(l.`U-PRO`) LIKE '+3(%' OR TRIM(l.`U-PRO`) LIKE '+4(%')));
answer:
The eligibility count is **4** patients.

This is the union of two groups that do not overlap: 3 patients with an abnormal fibrinogen (FG below 150 or above 450) and 1 patient with a severe proteinuria result. The query returns one column, `eligible_patient_count`.

Readings I chose:
- "Born after 1980-01-01" is strictly after, so a birthday of exactly 1980-01-01 is excluded. Patients with no birthday are excluded.
- Fibrinogen is abnormal only when FG < 150 or FG > 450, so exactly 150 and 450 are normal.
- Severe proteinuria is U-PRO coded as 3+ or 4+ (300 mg/dl or more). I counted the grade codes `3`, `4`, `%%` (the dataset's saturated reading, per the verified-query notes), and the mg/dl forms `300`, `>=300`, `>=1000`, and `+3(...)`/`+4(...)`. Among patients born after 1980, only the code `3` actually appears, so the other codes don't change this result.
- `TR`, `-`, `0`, `1`, `2`, `30`, `100`, `+1(30)`, `+2(100)`, and `-15` are treated as not severe.

The query ran against `db.sqlite` and returned 4. A separate check gave 3 for fibrinogen alone and 1 for proteinuria alone.

sql: SELECT m.first_name, m.last_name FROM member AS m JOIN attendance AS a ON a.link_to_member = m.member_id GROUP BY m.member_id, m.first_name, m.last_name HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.link_to_event) > 7 ORDER BY m.member_id;
answer: The query returns 30 students who attended more than 7 events, as first_name and last_name columns. I read "students" as the rows in the member table, since the database has no separate student table, and I counted distinct events per member from the attendance table. The top attendees are Elijah Allen and Phillip Cullen with 16 events each. I ordered the results by member_id, which the question did not specify.

sql: WITH q3t AS (SELECT d.driverRef, CAST(substr(q.q3,1,instr(q.q3,':')-1) AS INTEGER)*60000 + CAST(replace(substr(q.q3,instr(q.q3,':')+1),'.','') AS INTEGER) AS ms FROM qualifying q JOIN races r ON r.raceId=q.raceId JOIN drivers d ON d.driverId=q.driverId WHERE r.year=2017 AND r.name='Italian Grand Prix' AND q.q3 IS NOT NULL AND q.q3<>'') SELECT driverRef FROM q3t WHERE ms=(SELECT MIN(ms) FROM q3t);
answer: The driver with the fastest Q3 time at the 2017 Italian Grand Prix is `hamilton` (1:35.554). No other driver set the same time, so there is one result row. I matched the race by year 2017 and name 'Italian Grand Prix' (raceId 981), and compared Q3 times as milliseconds because they are stored as text.

sql: SELECT d.department, COALESCE(SUM(i.amount), 0) AS total_dues FROM (SELECT DISTINCT department FROM major WHERE college = 'College of Engineering') AS d LEFT JOIN major AS mj ON mj.department = d.department LEFT JOIN member AS m ON m.link_to_major = mj.major_id LEFT JOIN income AS i ON i.link_to_member = m.member_id AND i.source = 'Dues' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM attendance AS a JOIN event AS e ON e.event_id = a.link_to_event WHERE a.link_to_member = m.member_id) GROUP BY d.department ORDER BY d.department;
answer:
Query run against db.sqlite returns four rows, one per department in the College of Engineering:

- Civil and Environmental Engineering Department: 200
- Electrical and Computer Engineering Department: 50
- Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering Department: 0

Interpretation I chose:

sql:
SELECT s.School, s.StreetAbr
FROM schools AS s
JOIN frpm AS f ON f.CDSCode = s.CDSCode
WHERE s.School IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(s.School) <> ''
  AND (s.GSserved = 'K' OR s.GSserved GLOB 'K-*' OR s.GSserved GLOB '[0-9]*')
  AND CASE
        WHEN s.GSserved = 'K' THEN 0
        WHEN s.GSserved GLOB 'K-*' THEN CAST(substr(s.GSserved, 3) AS INTEGER)
        ELSE CAST(substr(s.GSserved, instr(s.GSserved, '-') + 1) AS INTEGER)
      END <= 8
  AND f."Enrollment (K-12)" - f."Enrollment (Ages 5-17)" > 30
ORDER BY s.School;
answer:
The query returns 120 schools, one row each, with columns School and StreetAbr. I ran it read-only and the output has 120 data rows.

Readings I chose:
- "Highest grade of enrollment" is taken from schools.GSserved, since the docs define GSserved as the highest grade of student enrollment. The frpm "High Grade" column disagrees with GSserved on about 9,900 rows, so using it instead would give a different list.
- "Grade 8 or below" parses the high grade from GSserved. K counts as 0, and ranges like "K-5" or "6-8" use the number after the dash. Values with no K-12 grade (P, Adult, Post Secondary) and blank values are excluded.
- "Street address" is schools.StreetAbr, the field the docs label as the street address. No qualifying school has a blank StreetAbr.
- "Named school" means School is not null and not blank.
- Schools with a missing K-12 or ages 5-17 enrollment are excluded, because the difference cannot be computed for them.
- The query applies no school-type filter beyond the grade condition, so it includes any school whose highest grade is 8 or below, including the K-8 charter and K-8 schools.

sql:
SELECT e.Symptoms AS symptom
FROM Examination AS e
INNER JOIN Patient AS p ON e.ID = p.ID
WHERE e.Thrombosis > 0
  AND e.Symptoms IS NOT NULL
  AND TRIM(e.Symptoms) <> ''
  AND (',' || REPLACE(REPLACE(p.Diagnosis, ' ', ''), CHAR(29), ',') || ',') LIKE '%,SLE,%'
GROUP BY e.Symptoms
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, e.Symptoms ASC
LIMIT 1
answer:
CNS lupus

The query returned one row. CNS lupus appears in 2 thrombotic episodes, and every other symptom appears once (CNS susp, thrombocytopenia, thrombophlebitis), so there is no tie.

How I read the question:
- "Thrombotic episode" is not a modeled Term. I used the Special Examination rows (Examination table) with Thrombosis > 0, meaning thrombosis degree 1, 2 or 3. Each row is one episode, with no date filter.
- "Diagnosed with SLE" uses Patient.Diagnosis, the patient's own diagnosis record. A patient counts only if SLE appears as a whole item in that list, so "SLE susp" is excluded. Examination.Diagnosis was not used.
- Symptoms are counted as recorded, including "CNS susp", which is a suspected symptom. Rows with no symptom were left out.

Caveat: the result rests on very few episodes. Only 5 SLE-patient thrombotic episodes have a symptom recorded, and the Terms used (Patient, Special Examination) are draft, not certified.

sql: SELECT DISTINCT b.bond_id FROM bond AS b JOIN connected AS c ON c.bond_id = b.bond_id JOIN atom AS a1 ON a1.atom_id = c.atom_id JOIN atom AS a2 ON a2.atom_id = c.atom_id2 WHERE (a1.element = 'p' AND a2.element = 'n') OR (a1.element = 'n' AND a2.element = 'p') ORDER BY b.bond_id
answer: Six bonds join a phosphorus atom and a nitrogen atom: TR032_2_3, TR032_3_5, TR058_1_3, TR058_1_4, TR058_1_5, and TR298_1_5. All are single bonds ('-'). I read the question as bonds whose two endpoint atoms are one 'p' and one 'n', and returned only bond_id. Each bond appears twice in the connected table, so the query uses DISTINCT. The query was run against db.sqlite and returned these six rows.

sql: WITH first_posts AS (SELECT OwnerUserId, MIN(CreaionDate) AS first_post_date FROM posts WHERE OwnerUserId IS NOT NULL GROUP BY OwnerUserId) SELECT COUNT(*) AS user_count FROM first_posts AS f INNER JOIN users AS u ON u.Id = f.OwnerUserId WHERE f.first_post_date >= '2010-01-01' AND f.first_post_date < '2011-01-01' AND (trim(u.Location) = 'India' OR (instr(u.Location, ',') > 0 AND trim(substr(u.Location, instr(u.Location, ',') + 1)) = 'India'))
answer:
12 users whose first post was created in calendar year 2010 are located in India.

How I read the question:
- "First post" means each user's earliest post by posts.CreaionDate (OwnerUserId = the user). A user counts only if that earliest date falls in 2010, so a user whose later posts are in 2010 but whose first post was earlier is excluded.
- "Located in India" uses the ontology's strict India filter: Location is exactly 'India', or its last comma-separated part is 'India' (e.g. 'Mumbai, India'). Places that only contain the word, such as 'Indiana' and 'Indianapolis, IN', are not counted.

The query ran without truncation. The Post and User Terms it relies on are draft, not certified. I have not saved this as a verified example yet; tell me if the reading is right and I will save it.

sql:
SELECT s.type AS set_type,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM set_translations t WHERE t.setCode = s.code AND t.translation IS NOT NULL) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS translated_set_count,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM set_translations t WHERE t.setCode = s.code AND t.translation IS NOT NULL) THEN s.totalSetSize ELSE 0 END), 0) AS total_card_count
FROM sets AS s
GROUP BY s.type
ORDER BY s.type

The query returns 20 set types, sorted alphabetically. Across all types, 121 sets have an official translated name, and the translated-set counts sum to that. Types with no translated set (funny, masterpiece, memorabilia, promo, spellbook, starter, token, treasure_chest, vanguard) show 0 and 0.

Interpretation choices:
- "Officially translated name" means a `set_translations` row with `translation IS NOT NULL`, counted once per set (a set with several languages counts once). Empty strings don't occur in the data.
- "Total number of cards in those sets" is the sum of `sets.totalSetSize` over the translated sets. The docs define that column as the total card count of the set, including promos and supplemental products. I did not count `cards` rows, because 15 sets have no rows there and the counts would differ. If you meant printings actually in the `cards` table, the query would need to change.

Results (set_type, translated_set_count, total_card_count): archenemy 1/150, box 3/284, commander 7/2031, core 13/4584, draft_innovation 2/432, duel_deck 18/1363, expansion 61/14023, from_the_vault 8/126, funny 0/0, masterpiece 0/0, masters 5/1121, memorabilia 0/0, planechase 2/312, premium_deck 1/34, promo 0/0, spellbook 0/0, starter 0/0, token 0/0, treasure_chest 0/0, vanguard 0/0.

sql:

  FROM Patient AS p
  JOIN Laboratory AS l ON l.ID = p.ID

FROM cand

sql: WITH tri_el AS (SELECT DISTINCT a.element AS element FROM connected AS c JOIN bond AS b ON b.bond_id = c.bond_id JOIN atom AS a ON a.atom_id = c.atom_id WHERE b.bond_type = '#') SELECT a.element AS element, COUNT(DISTINCT a.molecule_id) AS molecule_count FROM atom AS a JOIN tri_el AS t ON t.element = a.element GROUP BY a.element ORDER BY molecule_count DESC, a.element ASC;

sql:
WITH hero_powers AS (
  SELECT s.id AS hero_id, s.gender_id, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT hp.power_id) FROM hero_power AS hp WHERE hp.hero_id = s.id) AS power_count
  FROM superhero AS s
  WHERE s.full_name IS NOT NULL AND s.full_name <> '-'

JOIN gender AS g ON g.id = h.gender_id
WHERE g.gender IN ('Male', 'Female')
GROUP BY g.gender

sql: SELECT a.element, SUM(CASE WHEN a.atom_id IN (SELECT atom_id FROM connected UNION SELECT atom_id2 FROM connected) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS bonded_atoms FROM atom AS a WHERE a.molecule_id = 'TR397' GROUP BY a.element ORDER BY a.element

sql: WITH counts AS (SELECT a.element, COUNT(*) AS occurrences FROM atom AS a JOIN molecule AS m ON m.molecule_id = a.molecule_id WHERE m.label = '-' GROUP BY a.element) SELECT element FROM counts WHERE occurrences = (SELECT MIN(occurrences) FROM counts) ORDER BY element;

sql: WITH race AS (SELECT raceId FROM races WHERE year = 1988 AND name = 'Australian Grand Prix'), win AS (SELECT x.milliseconds AS ms, x.laps AS laps FROM results AS x WHERE x.raceId = (SELECT raceId FROM race) AND x.positionOrder = 1), last AS (SELECT x.milliseconds AS ms FROM results AS x WHERE x.raceId = (SELECT raceId FROM race) AND x.milliseconds IS NOT NULL AND x.laps = (SELECT laps FROM win) ORDER BY x.positionOrder DESC LIMIT 1) SELECT ROUND(100.0 * ((SELECT ms FROM last) - (SELECT ms FROM win)) / (SELECT ms FROM last), 2) AS pct_shorter FROM (SELECT 1);
answer:
The result is 1.16. The winner's elapsed time (Michael... no: driverId 117, 6,794,676 ms) was 1.16% shorter than the last full-distance finisher's time (driverId 119, 6,874,764 ms), using (6,874,764 − 6,794,676) / 6,874,764 × 100 = 1.1649%.

Interpretation choices:
- "Elapsed time" is `results.milliseconds`, because the `time` text is only a gap for non-winners.
- "Last full-distance finisher" means the lowest-placed classified finisher who completed the same 82 laps as the winner. The lapped cars (+1 Lap, +2 Laps) completed 81 or 80 laps, so I excluded them. That makes position 4 (driverId 119) the last full-distance finisher.
- The query uses the `positionOrder` column for finishing order, as the wiki recommends.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS patient_count FROM Patient AS p WHERE p.Admission = '-' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND l.RA IN ('-', '+-')) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Examination AS e WHERE e.ID = p.ID AND (e.KCT = '+' OR e.RVVT = '+' OR e.LAC = '+'));

- "Normal RF" means at least one laboratory record has RA '-' or '+-'.
- "Outpatient" means `Patient.Admission = '-'`. Blank and '+(' values are not counted.
- "Thrombosis ward" is taken to mean the whole database, since no ward field exists.

sql:
WITH acc AS (
  SELECT a.account_id, a.district_id, substr(a.date, 1, 4) AS yr
  FROM account AS a JOIN district AS d ON d.district_id = a.district_id
  WHERE d.A3 = 'central Bohemia' AND a.date >= '1996-01-01'
),
lent AS (SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS amt FROM loan GROUP BY account_id),
acc_amt AS (
  SELECT acc.yr, acc.district_id, COALESCE(l.amt, 0) AS amt
  FROM acc LEFT JOIN lent AS l ON l.account_id = acc.account_id
),
per_dist AS (
  SELECT yr, district_id, SUM(amt) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS per_acc FROM acc_amt GROUP BY yr, district_id
)
SELECT t.yr AS year, t.n AS accounts, t.total AS total_lent, ROUND(p.avg_pd, 2) AS avg_lent_per_account_by_district
FROM (SELECT yr, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amt) AS total FROM acc_amt GROUP BY yr) AS t
JOIN (SELECT yr, AVG(per_acc) AS avg_pd FROM per_dist GROUP BY yr) AS p ON p.yr = t.yr
ORDER BY t.yr;
answer:
The query returns two rows, one for 1996 and one for 1997 (the account dates run only through 1997-12-29).

- 1996: 191 accounts, total lent 4,887,024, average lent per account across districts 23639.03
- 1997: 114 accounts, total lent 1,971,468, average lent per account across districts 19809.53

Readings I chose where the question was open:
- "Average across the districts" is the unweighted mean of each district's own per-account average (total lent ÷ accounts opened in that district that year). Only districts with at least one account opened that year are included. Districts with no accounts that year are not counted as zero.
- Accounts with no loan count as 0 in both the total and the per-account averages.
- Each account has at most one loan in this data (682 loans, 682 distinct accounts), so the amount is that loan's amount.
- The region is matched on `district.A3 = 'central Bohemia'`, and the account date filter is `date >= '1996-01-01'`. Account dates are stored as text `YYYY-MM-DD`, so the year is `substr(date, 1, 4)`, which gives text like '1996'.
- The result has the year, the account count, the total, and the rounded average, in that order. I ran the query read-only and it returned the rows above.

sql:
WITH tabor AS (
  SELECT a.account_id, a.date AS opened
  FROM account AS a
  WHERE a.district_id = (SELECT d.district_id FROM district AS d WHERE d.A2 = 'Tabor')
    AND a.date <= '1996-12-31'
),
owner AS (
  SELECT dp.account_id, c.gender, c.birth_date
  FROM disp AS dp
  JOIN client AS c ON c.client_id = dp.client_id
  WHERE dp.type = 'OWNER'
),
cards AS (
  SELECT dp.account_id, COUNT(DISTINCT cd.card_id) AS card_count
  FROM card AS cd
  JOIN disp AS dp ON dp.disp_id = cd.disp_id
  WHERE cd.issued <= '1996-12-31'
  GROUP BY dp.account_id
),
loans AS (
  SELECT l.account_id,
         COUNT(*) AS loan_count,
         CASE
           WHEN COUNT(*) = 0 THEN 'no loan'
           WHEN SUM(CASE WHEN l.status = 'B' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0 THEN 'defaulted'
           WHEN SUM(CASE WHEN l.status IN ('C', 'D') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0 THEN 'repaying'
           ELSE 'paid off'
         END AS loan_label
  FROM loan AS l
  WHERE l.date <= '1996-12-31'
  GROUP BY l.account_id
),
tx97 AS (
  SELECT t.account_id,
         COUNT(*) AS tx_count,
         SUM(CASE WHEN t.type = 'PRIJEM' THEN t.amount ELSE 0 END) AS money_in,
         SUM(CASE WHEN t.type IN ('VYDAJ', 'VYBER') THEN t.amount ELSE 0 END) AS money_out,
         MAX(t.balance) AS peak_balance
  FROM trans AS t
  WHERE t.date >= '1997-01-01' AND t.date < '1998-01-01'
  GROUP BY t.account_id
),
profile AS (
  SELECT tb.account_id,
         tb.opened,
         o.gender,
         CAST(STRFTIME('%Y', '1996-12-31') AS INTEGER) - CAST(STRFTIME('%Y', o.birth_date) AS INTEGER)
           - CASE WHEN STRFTIME('%m-%d', '1996-12-31') < STRFTIME('%m-%d', o.birth_date) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS owner_age,
         COALESCE(cd.card_count, 0) AS card_count,
         COALESCE(ln.loan_count, 0) AS loan_count,
         COALESCE(ln.loan_label, 'no loan') AS loan_label,
         COALESCE(tx.tx_count, 0) AS tx_count,
         COALESCE(tx.money_in, 0) AS money_in,
         COALESCE(tx.money_out, 0) AS money_out,
         COALESCE(tx.peak_balance, 0) AS peak_balance
  FROM tabor AS tb
  LEFT JOIN owner AS o ON o.account_id = tb.account_id
  LEFT JOIN cards AS cd ON cd.account_id = tb.account_id
  LEFT JOIN loans AS ln ON ln.account_id = tb.account_id
  LEFT JOIN tx97 AS tx ON tx.account_id = tb.account_id
)
SELECT p.account_id,
       p.opened AS account_opened_date,
       p.gender AS owner_gender,
       p.owner_age,
       p.card_count,
       p.loan_count,
       p.loan_label,
       p.tx_count AS transactions_1997,
       p.money_in AS money_in_1997,
       p.money_out AS money_out_1997,
       p.peak_balance AS peak_balance_1997,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY p.peak_balance DESC) AS peak_balance_rank_1997
FROM profile AS p
ORDER BY peak_balance_rank_1997 ASC, p.account_id ASC
answer:
The query returns 37 rows, one per account held at the Tabor branch on or before 31 December 1996. It validated and ran without truncation.

Interpretation choices, since there was no one to ask:
- **Branch:** the Tabor district via `account.district_id`, which is the branch district, not the owner's home district.
- **Held as of 31 Dec 1996:** the account opening date is on or before 1996-12-31.
- **Owner:** the `OWNER` disposition. Gender and age come from that client. Age is completed years at 1996-12-31.
- **Cards:** distinct cards linked to any disposition on the account, issued on or before 1996-12-31. A card on a DISPONENT disposition counts toward the account.
- **Loans:** loans approved on or before 1996-12-31. The loan standing label uses each loan's current `loan.status`, as the question's status rules are written. It does not use the status as it stood in 1996, which the data does not record.
- **1997 activity:** transactions dated in calendar 1997. Money in is `PRIJEM`. Money out is `VYDAJ` plus `VYBER` (cash withdrawal). Count, money in, and money out are 0 when there is no activity.
- **Peak balance:** the maximum `trans.balance` in 1997, or 0 if there were no 1997 transactions. The rank is `RANK()` by this value, highest first, and the result is sorted by rank, then ascending account id.

Top results: account 7606 is rank 1 with a 1997 peak of 132,635, and account 2068 is last at 18,349. No two accounts tied on peak in this result, so no ranks are shared.

The ontology's Terms (Account, Client, Disposition, Loan, Credit Card, Transaction, District) are all draft, not certified, so the definitions behind these figures have not been reviewed by a person.

counts AS (SELECT c.name AS country_name, COUNT(lt.pid) AS player_count FROM Country AS c LEFT JOIN light AS lt ON lt.country_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name)
SELECT country_name FROM counts WHERE player_count = (SELECT MIN(player_count) FROM counts) ORDER BY country_name
answer:
Poland is the answer. It has the fewest distinct players weighing 160 lb or less who appeared in its league matches across all seasons: 206. There is no tie. The next lowest is Switzerland with 209.

Reading I chose: a player counts once per country, whichever match or season they appeared in. A player counts if they appear in any of the 22 starting-lineup slots (home_player_1–11 or away_player_1–11) of a match whose country_id is that country. I used the `Player.weight` column directly, since its values (117–243) are in pounds. Players with no recorded weight are excluded. Countries are grouped by `Match.country_id`, which matches each match's league country in every row.

The query returns only the country name, since that is what the question asks for. The per-country counts for all 11 countries were checked and are: Poland 206, Switzerland 209, Germany 250, Belgium 328, Italy 341, England 355, Netherlands 355, Scotland 356, Portugal 431, France 451, Spain 497.

sql:
WITH gold_owner AS (
  SELECT d.account_id, c.gender
  FROM card k
  JOIN disp d ON d.disp_id = k.disp_id AND d.type = 'OWNER'
  JOIN client c ON c.client_id = d.client_id
  WHERE k.type = 'gold'
),
high_bal AS (
  SELECT account_id FROM trans GROUP BY account_id HAVING AVG(balance) > 1000
),
gender_districts AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT g.gender, a.district_id
  FROM gold_owner g
  JOIN high_bal h ON h.account_id = g.account_id
  JOIN account a ON a.account_id = g.account_id
),
dist AS (
  SELECT gd.gender, di.district_id, di.A2 AS district, CAST(di.A4 AS INTEGER) AS inhabitants, di.A11 AS salary, di.A10 AS urban_ratio
  FROM gender_districts gd
  JOIN district di ON di.district_id = gd.district_id
  WHERE CAST(di.A4 AS INTEGER) > 100000
),
agg AS (
  SELECT gender, COUNT(*) AS district_count, MAX(inhabitants) AS max_inh,
         ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary, ROUND(AVG(urban_ratio), 2) AS avg_urban_ratio
  FROM dist GROUP BY gender
)
SELECT dist.gender, agg.district_count, dist.district, dist.inhabitants, agg.avg_salary, agg.avg_urban_ratio
FROM dist JOIN agg ON agg.gender = dist.gender
WHERE dist.inhabitants = agg.max_inh
ORDER BY CASE dist.gender WHEN 'F' THEN 1 WHEN 'M' THEN 2 END, dist.district;
answer:
Women (F): 16 qualifying districts. The most populous is Hl.m. Praha with 1,204,953 inhabitants. Average salary across the 16 districts is 9245.44, and average urban inhabitant ratio is 69.16.

Men (M): 22 qualifying districts. The most populous is Hl.m. Praha with 1,204,953 inhabitants. Average salary across the 22 districts is 9347.86, and average urban inhabitant ratio is 71.03.

The query returns two rows, one per gender, with women first. Prague has no tie for the top spot, so only one row per gender.

Readings I chose:
- Gold-card holder = the client on the OWNER `disp` row of a card with `type = 'gold'`. The card is always an OWNER row, so gender comes from `client.gender`.
- Average balance = `AVG(trans.balance)` per account, after each transaction, kept when strictly greater than 1000.
- Branch district = `account.district_id`. Districts are de-duplicated per gender before averaging.
- Inhabitants = `CAST(district.A4 AS INTEGER)`, kept when strictly greater than 100000. Salary is `A11`, urban ratio is `A10`.

The query was run read-only against `db.sqlite` and returned these two rows. The wiki was not edited.

sql: WITH pro AS (SELECT l.ID, l.Date, l."U-PRO" AS level, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.ID ORDER BY l.Date DESC) AS rn FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l."U-PRO" IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(l."U-PRO") <> '') SELECT p.ID AS patient_id, p.SEX AS sex, pro.Date AS test_date, pro.level AS proteinuria_level FROM pro INNER JOIN Patient AS p ON p.ID = pro.ID WHERE pro.rn = 1 ORDER BY p.ID
answer:
295 patients have a proteinuria test. The query returns one row per patient with patient_id, sex, test_date (most recent proteinuria test by date), and proteinuria_level (the raw U-PRO value on that test).

Choices I made:
- A proteinuria test is a Laboratory row with a non-empty U-PRO value.
- Proteinuria level is the stored text as recorded (for example '-', '0', 'TR', '30', '>=300', and some unusual entries such as '%%').
- Sex is kept as stored, so one patient (115562) has an empty sex value.

The Laboratory Test and Patient Terms are draft, not certified. The query validated and the row count was confirmed. The tool display showed the first 100 of the 295 rows.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e.ID) AS patient_count FROM Examination AS e INNER JOIN Patient AS p ON p.ID = e.ID WHERE e.Thrombosis > 0 AND e.`Examination Date` BETWEEN '1997-01-01' AND '1997-12-31'
answer: 3 patients (IDs 14872, 163109, 4395720). Readings: cohort = all patients in the Patient table; "showed thrombosis" = Thrombosis > 0 on an Examination row dated 1997-01-01 to 1997-12-31 inclusive; counted as distinct patients. One 1997-04-28 thrombosis row has a NULL ID and is excluded because it cannot be linked to a patient.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM account AS a JOIN district AS d ON d.district_id = a.district_id WHERE d.A3 = 'north Bohemia' AND a.date <= '1995-12-31' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM trans AS t WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id AND t.bank = 'AB');
answer: 32. sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS school_count FROM schools AS s LEFT JOIN satscores AS sat ON sat.cds = s.CDSCode WHERE s.StatusType = 'Active' AND s.EILCode = 'HS' AND COALESCE(sat.NumTstTakr, 0) = 0;
answer:
952 currently open high schools in California had zero SAT test takers.

Readings I chose:
- "Currently open" = `StatusType = 'Active'`.
- "High school" = `EILCode = 'HS'` (High School instruction level).
- "Public" is not a separate field in `schools`, so I counted every directory row that meets the two filters above. The directory covers public schools, and charter schools are included. A few non-district rows (4 Non-School Locations, 1 State Board of Education, 2 Statewide Benefit Charter) also carry the HS code. Dropping them would change the count by at most a handful.
- A school with no `satscores` row, or with `NumTstTakr = 0`, counts as zero test takers. Of the 952, most have no SAT row at all, and the rest have an explicit zero.

The query was run against `db.sqlite` and returned 952.

sql:
WITH localized AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT s.code FROM sets AS s
  JOIN set_translations AS t ON t.setCode = s.code
  WHERE s.releaseDate BETWEEN '2017-01-01' AND '2017-12-31'
    AND t.translation IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(t.translation) <> ''
),
qualifying_codes AS (
  SELECT code FROM localized
  UNION
  SELECT s.code FROM sets AS s JOIN localized AS l ON s.parentCode = l.code
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_cards FROM cards WHERE setCode IN (SELECT code FROM qualifying_codes);
answer:
The total is **1018** cards.

Three 2017 sets have a non-blank translated name: Aether Revolt (AER), Amonkhet (AKH), and Commander 2017 (C17). I also counted their related supplemental sets, linked through `parentCode`: Aether Revolt Promos (PAER), Amonkhet Invocations (MP2), Amonkhet Promos (PAKH), and Commander 2017 Oversized (OC17).

Per set, the card counts are AER 197 + PAER 65 = 262, AKH 302 + MP2 54 + PAKH 87 = 443, and C17 309 + OC17 4 = 313, which sum to 1018.

Choices I made:
- I counted actual card rows in `cards` for each set code, not the `totalSetSize` column. Using `totalSetSize` would give 992 (AKH's totalSetSize is 287 + 54 + 76 = 417, and C17's is 309 + 4 = 313).
- I ignored blank translation rows. Several languages have blank entries, so a set only counts if it has at least one real translated name.

I ran the query and it returns 1018.

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(t.total_cost), 2) AS mean_total_expense_per_event FROM (SELECT b.link_to_event AS event_id, SUM(x.cost) AS total_cost FROM expense x JOIN member m ON m.member_id = x.link_to_member JOIN budget b ON b.budget_id = x.link_to_budget WHERE m.first_name = 'Elijah' AND m.last_name = 'Allen' AND strftime('%m', x.expense_date) IN ('09', '10') GROUP BY b.link_to_event) t;
answer:
Elijah Allen's mean total expense per event for September and October 2019 expenses is 98.77.

The query sums his expenses per event (expense → budget → event, grouped by event_id), then averages those totals across the six events involved. The per-event totals are: Registration 295.12, September Speaker 119.33, Yearly Kickoff 131.77, Officers meeting - September 20.20, Officers meeting - October 20.20, October Speaker 6.00. The sum is 592.62, and 592.62 / 6 = 98.77.

Interpretation: I read "mean total expense per event" as the average of each event's summed expenses, not the average cost of individual expense rows. Under the per-row reading the answer would be 74.08 (592.62 / 8). Every expense in the window resolves to an event, and I grouped by event_id rather than name, since names can repeat in this database. I ran the query read-only and did not edit the wiki.

sql: WITH rnp AS (SELECT p.ID, MAX(CAST(l.RNP AS REAL)) AS mx FROM Patient AS p JOIN Laboratory AS l ON l.ID = p.ID WHERE p.SEX = 'F' AND l.RNP IS NOT NULL GROUP BY p.ID) SELECT ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN mx > 64 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS percentage FROM rnp;
answer:
결과: 5.49 (5 / 91 × 100 = 5.4945…, 소수 둘째 자리 반올림)

선택한 해석은 다음과 같습니다.
- 코호트는 Patient 테이블 전체(1,238명)이고, 여성은 SEX = 'F'입니다.
- 분모는 RNP 결과가 하나 이상 기록된 여성 환자 91명입니다. 'negative'와 '0'도 결과가 있는 것으로 셉니다.
- 분자는 그중 RNP 결과 중 하나라도 64보다 큰 값이 있는 환자 5명입니다. 'negative'와 '0'은 수치로 0이 되어 상승으로 세지 않습니다.
- '가장 최근 결과'가 아니라 '전체 검사 기록 중 한 번이라도 상승'으로 판단했습니다. 최근 결과 기준으로 보면 값이 달라질 수 있습니다.
- RNP 값은 모두 숫자 또는 'negative'라서 CAST로 비교해도 안전합니다. 쿼리를 실행해 5.49를 확인했습니다.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.ID) AS patient_count FROM Patient AS p JOIN Laboratory AS l ON l.ID = p.ID WHERE p.SEX = 'F' AND l.WBC > 3.5 AND l.WBC < 9.0 AND (l.FG < 150 OR l.FG > 450) AND CAST(l.RNP AS REAL) > 15;
answer:
The answer is 1 (patient 4649885). Only one female patient has a single laboratory record (1993-10-04) that meets all three conditions: WBC 3.6, which is normal, FG 45.3, which is abnormal, and RNP 256, which is above 15.

Choices I made:
- The three conditions must hold on the same laboratory row, following the wiki's "same laboratory record" rule. The question's "a laboratory record showing" supports this reading.
- Normal WBC is 3.5 < WBC < 9.0, the documented range. Abnormal FG is FG < 150 or FG > 450, the confirmed rule from verified query 24. Raised RNP is strictly above 15, so the single RNP value of exactly 15 is excluded.
- Using an inclusive WBC range (3.5 to 9.0) gives the same count of 1, so the boundary choice does not affect the result.
- All laboratory dates are considered, with no date restriction.
- Female means Patient.SEX = 'F'.

The query was run read-only against db.sqlite and returned 1.

sql: WITH t AS (SELECT home_player_3 AS pid, SUM(home_team_goal) AS total FROM Match WHERE home_player_3 IS NOT NULL GROUP BY home_player_3) SELECT ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS avg_total_home_goals FROM t
answer:
The answer is 16.12.

Reading I chose: "the home team's third listed player" is the `home_player_3` column, the same slot used in verified query 8. "The whole player population" is the players who were `home_player_3` in at least one match, which is 2,375 players. Each one's total is the sum of `home_team_goal` over their matches in that slot, and the result is the average of those totals. Players with no such match are excluded, since they have no total to average. If you instead want every player in the `Player` table averaged in, with zero for those never in slot 3, the result would be lower; I did not compute that variant.

The query ran read-only against `db.sqlite` and returned 16.12. All 2,375 players have a non-null total, and every `home_player_3` ID exists in `Player`. Rows with a null goal value are ignored by `SUM`.

sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT DISTINCT a.district_id FROM client AS c JOIN disp AS x ON x.client_id = c.client_id JOIN account AS a ON a.account_id = x.account_id WHERE c.gender = 'F' AND c.birth_date < '1930-01-01') SELECT ROUND(AVG(d.A11), 2) AS average_salary FROM district AS d WHERE d.district_id IN (SELECT district_id FROM cohort);
answer:
The average salary across the districts is 9045.64. This comes from 75 distinct branch districts.

Reading I chose:
- Clients are female (gender = 'F') with birth_date before 1930-01-01.
- Their accounts are found through any disposition type (OWNER or DISPONENT), and the branch is the account's district_id.
- "The average salary of those districts" averages each distinct district once, not once per account. This matches how the earlier verified queries treat district sets.

The query returned 9045.64, and a check on the same set gave 75 districts with an unrounded average of 9045.64.

sql: SELECT DISTINCT name FROM cards WHERE isPromo = 1 AND side IS NOT NULL AND CAST(frameVersion AS INTEGER) = (SELECT MAX(CAST(frameVersion AS INTEGER)) FROM cards) ORDER BY name
answer: The query returns 127 distinct card names: promotional printings (isPromo = 1) of multi-face cards (side IS NOT NULL) that carry the latest frame year. The latest year is 2015, taken as the maximum of CAST(frameVersion AS INTEGER) over all cards. 'future' is excluded because the ontology casts it to 0. If 'future' should count as the newest frame style, the list would change; I did not run that variant. Multi-face names are returned as stored, with face names joined by " // ". The result was not truncated. The Card Term used is a draft, not certified.

sql: SELECT SUM(convertedManaCost) AS total_converted_mana_cost FROM cards WHERE artist = 'Rob Alexander' AND originalReleaseDate LIKE '2013/%';
answer:
The total converted mana cost is **4**. Only one card matches: Door of Destinies (Rob Alexander, original release 2013/1/11, converted mana cost 4.0).

Choices I made:
- Artist matched exactly as 'Rob Alexander'. Other Alexander artists (e.g., 'D. Alexander Gregory', 'Alexander Forssberg') are excluded.
- Dates are stored as slash-separated, non-zero-padded strings (e.g., '2013/1/11'), so the filter is `originalReleaseDate LIKE '2013/%'`. I confirmed no dates use another separator. Cards with a NULL original release date are excluded.
- Each printing is counted separately, with no DISTINCT.
- The question's "special-release" framing isn't a filter in the question's criteria, so I did not restrict to promo or special printings.

Query result: 4.0 (the single value `4.0`).

The administrator is Zachary Larsen, at Mission San Jose High (CDS 01611760135244) in Alameda County. That school has 421 test takers scoring at least 1500, the most of any school in the county with a school-level SAT record. The CDS code you gave is Berkeley High in Alameda County.

sql: SELECT ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN x.laps = w.laps THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2) FROM results AS x JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = x.driverId JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = x.raceId JOIN results AS w ON w.raceId = x.raceId AND w.positionOrder = 1 WHERE d.nationality = 'Japanese' AND r.year BETWEEN 2007 AND 2009

sql: SELECT c.colour AS hair_colour FROM superhero AS s JOIN race AS r ON r.id = s.race_id JOIN colour AS c ON c.id = s.hair_colour_id WHERE r.race = 'Human' AND s.height_cm > 0 AND s.height_cm = (SELECT MIN(s2.height_cm) FROM superhero AS s2 JOIN race AS r2 ON r2.id = s2.race_id WHERE r2.race = 'Human' AND s2.height_cm > 0);

sql: WITH lost AS (SELECT id, season, away_player_1 AS pid FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_2 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_3 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_4 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_5 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_6 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_7 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_8 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_9 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_10 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5 UNION ALL SELECT id, season, away_player_11 FROM Match WHERE home_team_goal - away_team_goal >= 5) SELECT season, COUNT(DISTINCT pid) AS player_count FROM lost WHERE pid IS NOT NULL GROUP BY season ORDER BY season
answer:
Eight seasons had at least one away-side loss by five or more goals. Distinct away-lineup players per season:

| season | player_count |
|---|---|
| 2008/2009 | 242 |
| 2009/2010 | 320 |
| 2010/2011 | 465 |
| 2011/2012 | 525 |
| 2012/2013 | 420 |

How I read the question:

- "Players in the away team's lineup" means the away_player_1 to away_player_11 slots only. Home players are excluded.
- Each player is counted once per season, and empty lineup slots are ignored.

The Match term is still draft (not certified), so the figures rest on that draft mapping. The result has 8 rows and was not truncated. I have not saved this as a verified example, since you have not confirmed it yet.

sql: SELECT d.code FROM qualifying AS q JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = q.raceId JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = q.driverId WHERE r.year = 2017 AND r.name = 'Italian Grand Prix' AND q.q3 IS NOT NULL AND q.q3 <> '' ORDER BY d.code;

sql: SELECT DISTINCT p.ID, p.Diagnosis, l.DNA FROM Patient AS p JOIN Laboratory AS l ON l.ID = p.ID WHERE instr(',' || REPLACE(p.Diagnosis, ' ', '') || ',', ',SLE,') > 0 AND l.DNA IS NOT NULL AND CAST(l.DNA AS REAL) = (SELECT MAX(CAST(l2.DNA AS REAL)) FROM Laboratory AS l2 JOIN Patient AS p2 ON p2.ID = l2.ID WHERE instr(',' || REPLACE(p2.Diagnosis, ' ', '') || ',', ',SLE,') > 0 AND l2.DNA IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY p.ID
answer: Patient 2933261 (diagnosis SLE) has the strongest anti-DNA result among patients with a confirmed SLE diagnosis: 185. No other patient ties. Readings used: confirmed SLE means the item SLE in the diagnosis list, excluding "susp"; anti-DNA is Laboratory.DNA, compared numerically and returned as written. Patient and Laboratory Test Terms are still draft. The query ran without truncation.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS patient_count FROM Patient AS p WHERE p.Birthday > '1960-01-01' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND CAST(l.RNP AS REAL) > 10);
answer:
594 patients were born after 1 January 1960 and never had a raised RNP result.

Choices I made:
- Cohort: all rows in `Patient`, since the database is the thrombosis cohort (the same convention the verified queries use). "After" is strict, so anyone born on 1960-01-01 is excluded. That date matches no patient.
- Raised: `CAST(RNP AS REAL) > 10`. The recorded RNP values are 0, 1, 4, 15, 16, 64, 256, and "negative". Only 15, 16, 64, and 256 are raised. "negative" casts to 0, so it is never raised. Empty RNP values are not raised.
- Patients with no laboratory rows are counted as never raised, via `NOT EXISTS`.

Check: 603 patients were born after the cutoff. 594 of them never had a raised RNP result, so 9 did. The query was run read-only against `db.sqlite` and returned 594.

sql: SELECT p.Diagnosis FROM Patient AS p WHERE p.Admission LIKE '%+%' AND p.`First Date` BETWEEN '1998-02-15' AND '1998-02-28' AND p.Birthday IS NOT NULL ORDER BY p.Birthday ASC, p.ID ASC LIMIT 1;
answer:
The oldest inpatient at first presentation in the 15–28 February 1998 window is patient 5765821 (born 1938-01-05, first visit 1998-02-27, age 60). Her diagnosis is `WG^]SJS`, returned exactly as stored. The `^]` is a literal 0x1D control character in the data, so I left it as is.

Readings I chose:
- "Inpatient" means any Admission value containing a plus sign, so `+(` counts. This follows the convention in the verified query for "admitted" (question 13). If you only want the exact value `+`, the answer changes to patient 5761409, diagnosis `BEHCET` (born 1985-09-08, first visit 1998-02-17).
- Age is computed from Birthday against the First Date of the visit. No ties occurred, so the ID tie-break was not needed.

The query was run and returned one row.

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(s.weight_kg), 1) AS average_weight_kg FROM superhero AS s JOIN colour AS c ON c.id = s.skin_colour_id WHERE c.colour = 'Green' AND s.weight_kg > 0
answer: The average weight of green-skinned heroes with a known weight is 1354.6 kg. I counted skin colour 'Green' only (id 14) and left out 'Green/Blue' (id 15), since it is a separate category. Weight counts as known when weight_kg > 0, which excludes NULL and 0. This leaves 21 heroes. The average is pulled up hard by Fin Fang Foom at 18000 kg. I kept him because the question asked for all heroes with a known weight, but without him the average would be much lower. sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS patient_count FROM Patient AS p WHERE p.Birthday > '1960-01-01' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND CAST(l.RNP AS REAL) > 10)

sql: WITH payer AS (SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID FROM transactions_1k WHERE Date = '2012-08-25' AND Price = 634.8), totals AS (SELECT SUBSTR(y.Date,1,4) AS yr, SUM(y.Consumption) AS tot FROM yearmonth AS y JOIN payer AS p ON p.CustomerID = y.CustomerID WHERE SUBSTR(y.Date,1,4) IN ('2012','2013') GROUP BY yr) SELECT ROUND((t13.tot - t12.tot) / t12.tot, 4) AS relative_change FROM (SELECT tot FROM totals WHERE yr = '2013') AS t13, (SELECT tot FROM totals WHERE yr = '2012') AS t12;

The relative change is **5.8152**.

Reading choices:
- "Price" is the `transactions_1k.Price` column, and the payment is matched on Date = '2012-08-25' and Price = 634.8.
- "Annual total" is the calendar-year sum of `yearmonth.Consumption`, including zero and negative months, as the verified queries do.

sql: WITH s2016 AS (SELECT s.code FROM sets s WHERE strftime('%Y', s.releaseDate) = '2016'), per_set AS (SELECT s.code, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN st.translation IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(st.translation) <> '' THEN st.language END) AS n_langs FROM s2016 s LEFT JOIN set_translations st ON st.setCode = s.code GROUP BY s.code) SELECT ROUND(AVG(n_langs), 2) AS avg_translated_languages FROM per_set;

4.74

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN s.height_cm > 0 THEN s.height_cm END), 2) AS avg_height_cm, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN s.weight_kg > 0 THEN s.weight_kg END), 2) AS avg_weight_kg FROM superhero AS s JOIN colour AS c ON c.id = s.skin_colour_id JOIN alignment AS a ON a.id = s.alignment_id WHERE c.colour = 'Green' AND a.alignment = 'Bad'

sql:
WITH owners AS (
  SELECT d.client_id, d.account_id, a.district_id
  FROM disp d
  JOIN card c ON c.disp_id = d.disp_id AND c.type = 'classic'
  JOIN account a ON a.account_id = d.account_id
  WHERE d.type = 'OWNER'
),
client_counts AS (
  SELECT district_id, COUNT(DISTINCT client_id) AS n_clients
  FROM owners GROUP BY district_id
),
pays AS (
  SELECT o.district_id, t.bank, t.account, t.amount
  FROM owners o
  JOIN trans t ON t.account_id = o.account_id
  WHERE t.type = 'VYDAJ' AND t.bank IS NOT NULL AND t.account > 0
),
ext_counts AS (
  SELECT district_id, COUNT(*) AS n_ext
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT district_id, bank, account FROM pays)
  GROUP BY district_id
),
pay_totals AS (
  SELECT district_id, SUM(amount) AS total_paid
  FROM pays GROUP BY district_id
)
SELECT di.A2 AS district,
       COALESCE(cc.n_clients, 0) AS classic_card_clients,
       COALESCE(ec.n_ext, 0) AS external_accounts_paid,
       COALESCE(pt.total_paid, 0) AS total_amount_paid
FROM district di
LEFT JOIN client_counts cc ON cc.district_id = di.district_id
LEFT JOIN ext_counts ec ON ec.district_id = di.district_id
LEFT JOIN pay_totals pt ON pt.district_id = di.district_id
ORDER BY total_amount_paid DESC, district ASC;
answer:
The query returns all 77 districts, ordered by total paid (highest first, then by name). Hl.m. Praha leads with 96 classic-card owners, 123 external accounts, and 14,125,240 paid. Olomouc is second at 3,235,882, and Breclav is last at 0 (2 clients, no external payments). Several districts have clients but no external payments, and they show zeros.

Readings I chose:
- "Classic-card-holding account owner" = a client with an OWNER disposition on an account, where the card on that same disposition row has type 'classic'. All 659 classic cards sit on owner dispositions, so this gives 659 clients and 659 accounts.
- "Outgoing payment" = `trans.type = 'VYDAJ'`. Only payments with a bank code and a counter-account above 0 count, because the question asks about payments sent outside the bank. That leaves 208,282 of the 634,571 VYDAJ rows. The other 426,289 have no counterparty, and I excluded them from both the count and the total.
- External accounts are distinct (bank, account) pairs per district, so one counterparty paid from two clients in the same district counts once.
- Totals are unrounded `SUM(amount)`, and the full history is used, with no date filter.

I ran the query against `db.sqlite` read-only and it returned 77 rows. I did not edit the wiki.

sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN g.Id IS NOT NULL THEN p.Score END) AS german_editor_total_score, SUM(CASE WHEN g.Id IS NULL THEN p.Score END) AS other_total_score, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT u.Id) FROM users u JOIN posts q ON q.LastEditorUserId = u.Id WHERE u.Location LIKE '%germany%' AND q.CreaionDate >= '2012-01-01' AND q.CreaionDate < '2013-01-01') AS german_editor_count, (SELECT SUM(u.Reputation) FROM users u WHERE u.Location LIKE '%germany%' AND u.Id IN (SELECT q.LastEditorUserId FROM posts q WHERE q.CreaionDate >= '2012-01-01' AND q.CreaionDate < '2013-01-01')) AS german_editor_reputation FROM posts p LEFT JOIN users g ON g.Id = p.LastEditorUserId AND g.Location LIKE '%germany%' WHERE p.CreaionDate >= '2012-01-01' AND p.CreaionDate < '2013-01-01';
answer:
결과는 한 행입니다: German-editor 2012 post score 349, other 2012 post score 63191, Germany-based last editors 32명, their combined reputation 26816.

Choices I made:
- 2012 기준은 `posts.CreaionDate`(원본 컬럼명 오타 그대로)를 2012-01-01 이상 2013-01-01 미만으로 잡았습니다.
- 독일 거주는 `Location`에 'germany'가 포함되는 경우로 판정했습니다(대소문자 무시). 'Berlin, Germany'와 'Germany'처럼 쉼표 뒤에 오는 형식뿐 아니라 'Aachen Germany'와 'Karlsruhe - Germany'도 잡힙니다. 'Germany / Philippines'처럼 독일과 다른 나라가 함께 적힌 경우도 포함됩니다. 이 값을 독일로 볼지는 보고서 기준에 따라 달라질 수 있습니다.
- "기타 게시글"에는 마지막 편집자가 없는(NULL) 게시글도 포함했습니다.
- 평판은 `users.Reputation` 값을 중복 없이(사용자별로 한 번씩) 합산했습니다.

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(s.weight_kg), 1) AS avg_weight_kg FROM superhero AS s JOIN colour AS c ON c.id = s.skin_colour_id WHERE c.colour = 'Green' AND s.weight_kg > 0
answer:
The average weight of green-skinned heroes with a recorded weight is **1354.6 kg**, based on 15 heroes.

Choices I made:
- "Green skin" means the skin colour `Green` (colour id 14). I left out the separate `Green/Blue` category (id 15), since it is a different value.
- A weight counts as known when `weight_kg > 0`, following the data dictionary, which says NULL or 0 means missing.

The result is driven by very heavy heroes in the data, so it reads high for a "typical" weight. The query is run and returns 1354.6.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS molecule_count FROM molecule m WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM atom a WHERE a.molecule_id = m.molecule_id AND a.element = 'n') AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM atom a JOIN connected c ON c.atom_id = a.atom_id OR c.atom_id2 = a.atom_id JOIN bond b ON b.bond_id = c.bond_id WHERE a.molecule_id = m.molecule_id AND a.element = 'n' AND b.bond_type IN ('=', '#'))
answer:
110 molecules qualify. Of the 187 molecules that contain at least one nitrogen (element 'n'), 77 have a nitrogen in a double ('=') or triple ('#') bond, which leaves 110. The query was run read-only against db.sqlite and returned 110.

Reading I took: a molecule is excluded if any of its nitrogen atoms has a double or triple bond to any neighbour. Aromatic or other bond types are not in the data (only '-', '=', '#' occur), so they don't affect the result. Bonds were looked up through the `connected` table in both atom directions, and I confirmed every connected row maps to a bond in the same molecule.

sql: WITH counts AS (SELECT p.publisher_name AS publisher_name, COUNT(s.id) AS hero_count FROM publisher AS p INNER JOIN superhero AS s ON s.publisher_id = p.id WHERE p.publisher_name IN ('Marvel Comics', 'DC Comics') GROUP BY p.publisher_name) SELECT (SELECT c.publisher_name FROM counts AS c ORDER BY c.hero_count DESC LIMIT 1) AS publisher, (SELECT MAX(c.hero_count) FROM counts AS c) - (SELECT MIN(c.hero_count) FROM counts AS c) AS difference
answer:
Marvel Comics has more superheroes than DC Comics, by 163. The query returned one row: publisher = Marvel Comics, difference = 163.

Reading I chose: "superheroes" means every row in the superhero table attributed to the publisher through superhero.publisher_id, with no filter on alignment, full name, or other attributes. The count is per publisher name in the publisher table. The Publisher and Superhero Terms are still draft (not certified). I ran the query once and did not check the two individual counts separately.

Water, on 10 food-budget purchase records.

Readings I chose:
- "Food budget only" means expenses linked to budget lines with `category = 'Food'` (22 lines).
- A "purchase record" is an expense row, and each comma-separated item in `expense_description` is split out. Counts are distinct expense records per item.
- Items are matched case-insensitively, so "Cookies" and "cookies" are one item. Without that folding, Water still wins with 10 records; the next-highest item, cookies, has 9 records once case is folded (6 + 3).

The query returns the item in lowercase (`water`) because of the case folding.

sql: SELECT ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN STRFTIME('%Y', Birthday) >= '1960' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS percentage FROM Patient WHERE LOWER(Diagnosis) = 'psoriatic arthritis';
answer: 50.0%. Two registry patients have a psoriatic arthritis diagnosis (`Patient.Diagnosis`), and one of them was born in 1960 or later (ID 3554252, born 1969-02-09; the other, ID 4547222, was born 1955-03-16).
