sql: WITH pairs AS (SELECT b.bond_type AS kind, MIN(a1.element, a2.element) AS e1, MAX(a1.element, a2.element) AS e2, b.bond_id FROM bond AS b JOIN connected AS c ON c.bond_id = b.bond_id JOIN atom AS a1 ON a1.atom_id = c.atom_id JOIN atom AS a2 ON a2.atom_id = c.atom_id2 WHERE b.molecule_id = 'TR377' AND b.bond_type IN ('-', '=') AND c.atom_id < c.atom_id2) SELECT p.kind AS bond_kind, COUNT(*) AS bond_count, COUNT(DISTINCT p.e1 || '-' || p.e2) AS element_pair_count, m.label AS carcinogenicity_label FROM pairs AS p JOIN molecule AS m ON m.molecule_id = 'TR377' GROUP BY p.kind ORDER BY bond_count DESC, bond_kind ASC;
answer:
Molecule TR377 has 12 single bonds ('-') and 4 double bonds ('='). Its carcinogenicity label is '-', so it is non-carcinogenic. The query returns:

| bond_kind | bond_count | element_pair_count | carcinogenicity_label |
|---|---|---|---|
| - | 12 | 3 | - |
| = | 4 | 1 | - |

Interpretation choices: I counted bonds from the `bond` table, where each bond is one row (the `connected` table stores each bond in both directions, so I kept only one direction per bond). I counted element pairs as distinct unordered element pairs, so a C–H bond and an H–C bond count as one pair. Single bonds join C–C, C–H and C–Cl (3 pairs), and double bonds join only C–C (1 pair). The result matches a manual count of the 16 bonds. The query is read-only and was run against `db.sqlite`.

sql: WITH seg AS (SELECT c.Segment AS segment, SUM(CASE WHEN SUBSTR(y.Date,1,4)='2013' THEN y.Consumption ELSE 0 END) AS c13, SUM(CASE WHEN SUBSTR(y.Date,1,4)='2012' THEN y.Consumption ELSE 0 END) AS c12 FROM customers AS c JOIN yearmonth AS y ON y.CustomerID = c.CustomerID WHERE c.Currency = 'EUR' AND c.Segment IN ('SME','LAM','KAM') GROUP BY c.Segment), pct AS (SELECT segment, ROUND((c13 - c12) * 100.0 / NULLIF(c12, 0), 2) AS increase_pct FROM seg), ext AS (SELECT MAX(increase_pct) AS mx, MIN(increase_pct) AS mn FROM pct) SELECT segment, increase_pct FROM pct, ext WHERE increase_pct = mx OR increase_pct = mn ORDER BY increase_pct DESC, segment
answer:
Highest: SME, +734.71%. Lowest: LAM, +539.83%. KAM (+553.21%) falls between them, so it is not in the result. No ties.

Interpretation: EUR-paying customers are those with Currency = 'EUR' in `customers`. Total consumption per segment is the sum of `yearmonth.Consumption` over all months of 2012 and of 2013. The increase is (2013 − 2012) / 2012 × 100, rounded to two decimals. The query returns two rows, highest first, with columns segment and increase_pct. I ran it against db.sqlite and it returned these two rows. I did not add it to verified_queries.md.

sql: SELECT DISTINCT p.ID AS patient_id, (2026 - CAST(STRFTIME('%Y', p.Birthday) AS INTEGER) - CASE WHEN STRFTIME('%m-%d', p.Birthday) > '10-09' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS age FROM Laboratory AS l JOIN Patient AS p ON p.ID = l.ID WHERE l.LDH > 600 AND l.LDH < 800 AND (l.`U-PRO` IN ('3','4') OR CAST(REPLACE(l.`U-PRO`, '>=', '') AS REAL) >= 300) ORDER BY p.ID
answer:
Three patients qualify: 3182521 (age 73), 4425292 (age 71), and 4632548 (age 99), ages completed as of 2026-10-09.

Readings chosen: both findings must fall on the same lab row (one patient, one test date). Plain numbers and '>=' values are mg/dL, and dipstick grades 3 and 4 count as at least 300. The grade choice doesn't change the list. Age is 2026 minus birth year, minus 1 if the birthday is after 10-09. The Patient and Laboratory Test terms are still draft (not certified).

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN s.height_cm > 0 THEN s.height_cm END), 1) AS avg_height_cm, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN s.weight_kg > 0 THEN s.weight_kg END), 1) AS avg_weight_kg FROM superhero AS s INNER JOIN publisher AS p ON s.publisher_id = p.id WHERE p.publisher_name = 'George Lucas'
answer:
George Lucas의 히어로(publisher_name = 'George Lucas')를 기준으로 계산한 결과입니다.

- 평균 키: 187.2 cm (height_cm > 0인 히어로만 포함)
- 평균 몸무게: 83.0 kg (weight_kg > 0인 히어로만 포함)

해석 및 선택한 기준:
- "만든 히어로"는 superhero.publisher_id가 George Lucas 출판사인 히어로로 해석했습니다.
- 키와 몸무게는 각각 독립적으로 평균을 냈습니다. 키가 없는 히어로도 몸무게가 있으면 몸무게 평균에는 들어갑니다.
- 키와 몸무게 평균 모두 히어로 수를 세지 않고 값이 있는 히어로만 계산했습니다. 키 평균에 포함된 히어로 수와 몸무게 평균에 포함된 히어로 수는 다를 수 있습니다.
- 초능력 보유 여부 조건은 질문에 없어서 적용하지 않았습니다.

사용한 Term(Superhero, Publisher)은 아직 certified 되지 않은 draft 상태입니다. 결과는 1행으로 잘리지 않았습니다.

sql: SELECT u.DisplayName FROM posts AS p JOIN users AS u ON p.LastEditorUserId = u.Id WHERE p.Title = 'Examples for teaching: Correlation does not mean causation'

The user who last edited "Examples for teaching: Correlation does not mean causation" has the display name **Abhilash**. The query returned one row, so the result is not truncated.

sql: SELECT CASE p.SEX WHEN 'F' THEN 'female' WHEN 'M' THEN 'male' END AS sex, COUNT(DISTINCT p.ID) AS patient_count FROM Patient AS p INNER JOIN Laboratory AS l ON l.ID = p.ID WHERE l.HGB < 10 AND p.SEX IN ('F','M') GROUP BY p.SEX ORDER BY p.SEX;
answer:
Result: female 87, male 11.

Reading I chose: "severe anemia" means a hemoglobin (HGB) value below 10 on any lab test, the same cutoff the wiki uses for anemia in confirmed query 27. A patient counts once if any of their lab rows has HGB < 10. Patients with a blank sex (13 rows) are excluded, since only F and M are labeled. The query is run read-only against db.sqlite and returns the two rows labeled 'female' and 'male'.

sql: SELECT CASE p.Admission WHEN '+' THEN 'admitted to the hospital' WHEN '-' THEN 'followed at the outpatient clinic' END AS patient_group, COUNT(*) AS normal_ldh_count FROM Laboratory AS l JOIN Patient AS p ON l.ID = p.ID WHERE p.Admission IN ('+', '-') AND l.LDH < 500 GROUP BY p.Admission ORDER BY CASE p.Admission WHEN '+' THEN 1 ELSE 2 END

sql: SELECT u.Id FROM users AS u WHERE u.DisplayName = 'Michael' AND u.Age IS NOT NULL ORDER BY u.Age ASC, u.Id ASC LIMIT 1

sql: SELECT CAST(frameVersion AS INTEGER) AS frame_year, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cards WHERE name = 'Tarmogoyf'), 2) AS pct_of_printings FROM cards WHERE name = 'Tarmogoyf' AND frameVersion = CAST(CAST(frameVersion AS INTEGER) AS TEXT) GROUP BY CAST(frameVersion AS INTEGER) ORDER BY frame_year DESC LIMIT 1

sql: WITH q3t AS (SELECT d.driverRef, q.q3, CAST(substr(q.q3, 1, instr(q.q3, ':') - 1) AS INTEGER) * 60000 + CAST(substr(q.q3, instr(q.q3, ':') + 1) AS REAL) * 1000 AS ms FROM qualifying AS q INNER JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = q.raceId INNER JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = q.driverId WHERE r.year = 2017 AND r.name = 'Italian Grand Prix' AND q.q3 IS NOT NULL AND q.q3 <> '') SELECT driverRef FROM q3t WHERE ms = (SELECT MIN(ms) FROM q3t)
answer:
The fastest Q3 time at the 2017 Italian Grand Prix was set by **hamilton**. This is one row, so there was no tie.

Method: I took every qualifying row for the 2017 Italian Grand Prix that has a Q3 time, converted the M:SS.mmm text to milliseconds, and kept the driver(s) with the minimum. I converted to milliseconds instead of comparing the text directly, so the result does not depend on the text format. The query returned one row, `hamilton`, and was not truncated.

The Terms used (Qualifying Result, Race, Driver) are still draft, not certified.

sql:
WITH documented AS (
  SELECT s.id, g.gender
  FROM superhero AS s
  JOIN gender AS g ON g.id = s.gender_id
  WHERE g.gender IN ('Male', 'Female')
    AND s.full_name IS NOT NULL AND s.full_name <> '-'
),
power_counts AS (
  SELECT d.gender, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM hero_power AS hp WHERE hp.hero_id = d.id) AS power_count
  FROM documented AS d
)
SELECT
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN gender = 'Male' THEN power_count END), 2) AS male_avg_superpowers,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN gender = 'Female' THEN power_count END), 2) AS female_avg_superpowers
FROM power_counts;
answer:
Male heroes with a documented full name: 8.49 average superpowers per hero (345 heroes). Female heroes with a documented full name: 6.83 (147 heroes).

Readings I chose: "documented full name" means full_name is neither NULL nor '-', the two encodings the data-quirks page lists. Heroes with no power records count as 0, so each average runs over every hero of that gender with a full name. Superpowers are counted as hero_power rows, which are all unique per hero and power. The query returns one row with two columns, male first.

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(convertedManaCost), 1) AS average_mana_value FROM (SELECT c.name, MAX(c.convertedManaCost) AS convertedManaCost FROM cards AS c WHERE c.edhrecRank BETWEEN 1 AND 1000 AND (',' || c.types || ',') LIKE '%,Creature,%' AND c.uuid IN (SELECT uuid FROM legalities WHERE status = 'Banned') GROUP BY c.name);
answer: The average mana value is 3.4, across 7 distinct creature cards that are banned in at least one format and have an EDHRec rank from 1 to 1000. I counted any format with a Banned status, treated "creature" as a whole token in `types`, and de-duplicated cards by name. The query returned 3.4 when run against db.sqlite. No verified query covers this question, so the result is checked only by running it.

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(s.weight_kg), 2) AS average_weight_kg FROM superhero AS s JOIN gender AS g ON s.gender_id = g.id JOIN alignment AS a ON s.alignment_id = a.id WHERE g.gender = 'Female' AND a.alignment = 'Good' AND s.weight_kg > 0;
answer:
The average weight of female superheroes with Good alignment is 70.76 kg (ROUND(AVG(weight_kg), 2)), based on 116 heroes. The query returned 70.76 when run read-only against db.sqlite.

Interpretation: "female" means gender = 'Female', "good" means alignment = 'Good', and "weight is known" means weight_kg > 0. Per data-quirks, 0 and NULL both mean missing, and `> 0` excludes both. I used inner joins on gender and alignment, which is safe here because the filter requires both values to be present.

sql: SELECT s.superhero_name FROM superhero AS s INNER JOIN colour AS c ON c.id = s.eye_colour_id WHERE c.colour = 'No Colour' AND s.height_cm BETWEEN 170 AND 190 ORDER BY s.id;
answer:
15 heroes match: Chuck Norris, Destroyer, Flash III, Goku, Green Goblin III, Indiana Jones, Judge Dredd, Mister Freeze, One Punch Man, Paul Blart, Robocop, Space Ghost, Stormtrooper, T-1000, Two-Face (listed in id order).

Interpretation: "recorded eye-colour category is unknown" is read as eye_colour = 'No Colour' (colour id 1), which the wiki and docs treat as the placeholder for none/unknown. Height 170 through 190 is inclusive, and BETWEEN excludes NULL and 0 heights automatically. Names are not deduplicated, though superhero_name is not unique in the table; this query returns one row per hero, and none of these 15 names repeats. I ran the query read-only against db.sqlite and it returned these 15 rows.

sql: SELECT s.code, s.releaseDate FROM sets AS s WHERE s.releaseDate >= '2020-01-01' AND s.releaseDate < '2021-01-01' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM set_translations AS st WHERE st.setCode = s.code AND st.language = 'Spanish' AND st.translation IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY s.releaseDate, s.code;
answer:
All 34 sets released in 2020 lack a Spanish name. The query returns 34 rows, which matches the total number of 2020 sets, because no 2020 set has a Spanish entry in set_translations. The 97 non-null Spanish translations in the table all belong to sets released in other years.

Choices I made:
- "Released in calendar year 2020" means releaseDate from 2020-01-01 up to but not including 2021-01-01. All releaseDate values are ISO format, so this is safe.
- "No Spanish name" means no set_translations row with language = 'Spanish' and a non-NULL translation. 24 Spanish rows have a NULL translation, and I counted those as missing. None of them belong to 2020 sets, so this choice does not change the result.
- Rows are ordered by release date, then set code. The question did not specify an order.
- Columns are set code (`code`) then release date (`releaseDate`), in the order asked.

The codes are: J20, PF20, PTHB, THB, UND, FMB1, HA2, C20, OC20, IKO, PIKO, PLGS, HA3, SLU, FJMP, SS3, M21, PM21, AJMP, JMP, 2XM, AKR, ANB, AZNR, MZNR, PZNR, SZNR, ZNC, ZNE, ZNR, PLIST, KLR, CMR, CC1.

sql: SELECT d.forename, COUNT(DISTINCT x.driverId) AS runners_up FROM results AS x JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = x.raceId JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = x.driverId WHERE r.name = 'Italian Grand Prix' AND x.positionOrder = 2 GROUP BY d.forename HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT x.driverId) >= 2 ORDER BY runners_up DESC, d.forename ASC
answer:
Two forenames recur among Italian Grand Prix runners-up across all editions: Mike (3 runners-up) and Juan (2 runners-up). The query returns these two rows.

Readings I chose:
- "Runners-up" are the drivers in position 2 (positionOrder = 2) in each Italian Grand Prix edition. I counted each driver once, so a driver who finished second more than once counts once. If you instead count each edition's second-place finish, the result changes: Mike becomes 4, Emerson, Jean, Jenson, Juan and Richie become 3, and 15 more forenames qualify with 2.
- "Italian Grand Prix" matches the race name exactly, across all years in the data (1950–2017).

sql: SELECT l.ID, l.Date, l.RNP FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.GOT >= 60 AND CAST(l.RNP AS REAL) = (SELECT MAX(CAST(l2.RNP AS REAL)) FROM Laboratory AS l2 WHERE l2.GOT >= 60);
answer:
The query returns one row: patient ID 1650222, lab test date 1989-07-18, anti-RNP reading 256. No other qualifying test ties at 256.

Readings I chose:
- "Above the normal range (60 or higher)" is `GOT >= 60`, as the question states, not the wiki's `GOT < 60` normal cutoff.
- The maximum is taken only over tests with GOT >= 60. Tests with a NULL GOT are excluded automatically.
- Anti-RNP is `Laboratory.RNP` cast to REAL, so `negative` counts as 0. The maximum is 256.
- The date is `Laboratory.Date`, the date the test was performed. The patient ID is `Laboratory.ID`, which matches `Patient.ID`, so no join to `Patient` is needed.

I ran the query read-only against `db.sqlite` and it returned the single row above. I did not edit the wiki.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS never_raised_rnp_patients FROM Patient AS p WHERE p.Birthday > '1960-01-01' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.ID = p.ID AND CAST(l.RNP AS REAL) > 10);
answer:
594

Query result: 594 patients born after 1 January 1960 never had a raised RNP result (strictly above 10).

Check: 603 patients in the Patient table were born after 1960, and 9 of them have at least one RNP result above 10, so 603 - 9 = 594.

Choices I made:
- The cohort is every row in `Patient`, since the database is the thrombosis cohort.
- Patients with no Laboratory rows count as never raised, as you specified.
- The one patient with a NULL Birthday is excluded, because there is no way to tell whether they were born after 1960.
- `CAST(RNP AS REAL)` turns `negative` into 0 and NULL stays NULL, so neither can count as raised. The only non-numeric RNP value is `negative`, so the cast is safe.

sql: WITH counts AS (SELECT p.publisher_name AS name, COUNT(s.id) AS n FROM publisher AS p LEFT JOIN superhero AS s ON s.publisher_id = p.id WHERE p.publisher_name IN ('DC Comics', 'Marvel Comics') GROUP BY p.publisher_name), diff AS (SELECT (SELECT n FROM counts WHERE name = 'Marvel Comics') - (SELECT n FROM counts WHERE name = 'DC Comics') AS d) SELECT CASE WHEN d > 0 THEN 'Marvel Comics' WHEN d < 0 THEN 'DC Comics' ELSE 'Tie' END AS publisher, ABS(d) AS difference FROM diff
answer: Marvel Comics has more superheroes than DC Comics, by 163 (387 Marvel vs. 224 DC). The query returns one row, `Marvel Comics | 163`, and returns `Tie` with 0 if the counts were equal. Heroes are counted by `superhero.publisher_id`. The three heroes with no publisher are not counted for either side. Height and weight are not filtered, since the question is about the number of heroes.

sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(y.Consumption), 2) AS avg_monthly_consumption FROM yearmonth AS y WHERE y.CustomerID = 15621 AND y.Date BETWEEN '201301' AND '201312' AND y.Consumption > 0
answer: 6.02. Customer 15621 averaged 6.02 units of fuel consumption per month across the 2013 months in which they had consumption above zero. "Fleet card" fuel consumption is yearmonth.Consumption, since no separate fleet-card measure exists; "actually purchased fuel" means Consumption > 0; 2013 is Date between 201301 and 201312. The Monthly Customer Consumption term is still draft, not certified. The query returned one row, not truncated.

sql: SELECT a2.element AS element, COUNT(DISTINCT c.bond_id) AS bond_count FROM connected AS c JOIN atom AS a1 ON a1.atom_id = c.atom_id JOIN atom AS a2 ON a2.atom_id = c.atom_id2 JOIN bond AS b ON b.bond_id = c.bond_id JOIN molecule AS m ON m.molecule_id = b.molecule_id WHERE a1.element = 'c' AND b.bond_type IN ('=', '#') AND m.label = '-' GROUP BY a2.element ORDER BY a2.element
answer:
Result (non-carcinogenic molecules, label '-'; double '=' and triple '#' bonds with one carbon end):

| element | bond_count |
|---|---|
| c | 553 |
| n | 27 |
| o | 103 |
| s | 11 |

Interpretation choices:
- "Non-carcinogenic" means molecule.label = '-'.
- "Double or triple" means bond_type IN ('=', '#'); single bonds are excluded.
- Each bond is counted once. The connected table stores every bond in both directions, so the query takes the direction where the first atom is carbon and counts COUNT(DISTINCT bond_id).
- Carbon itself is included as an element. A C=C bond joins a carbon atom to an atom of element 'c', so it counts under 'c' (553 bonds). If you want only heteroatoms, drop the 'c' row.
- Elements with no such bond do not appear. Hydrogen, halogens, and the other elements have zero qualifying bonds in this data.

The result has 4 rows and is not truncated. The Atom, Bond, and Molecule Terms are all draft (none certified). The query is validated and was run once with run_sql.

sql: WITH latest AS (SELECT p.player_name, a.player_api_id, a.overall_rating, a.defensive_work_rate, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY a.player_api_id ORDER BY a.date DESC, a.id DESC) AS rn FROM Player_Attributes AS a JOIN Player AS p ON p.player_api_id = a.player_api_id WHERE a.date < '2013-07-13 00:00:00'), cur AS (SELECT * FROM latest WHERE rn = 1), pop AS (SELECT overall_rating FROM cur WHERE defensive_work_rate IN ('low','medium','high') AND overall_rating IS NOT NULL) SELECT ROUND(100.0 * ((SELECT overall_rating FROM cur WHERE player_name = 'Landon Donovan') - AVG(overall_rating)) / AVG(overall_rating), 2) AS pct_higher FROM pop
answer:
18.67

Interpretation I chose: each player's overall rating "as of" 12 July 2013 is their most recent attribute record dated on or before that day (ties on the same date broken by higher id). The defensive work rate filter (low, medium or high) applies to that same record. The population is 9,928 players. Their average overall rating is 66.57, and Landon Donovan's rating on that date is 79 (his 2013-07-12 record, defensive work rate 'high'). (79 − 66.57) / 66.57 × 100 = 18.67%. The query returns one row, one column, and I ran it against db.sqlite and got 18.67.

sql: SELECT ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN u.Id IS NULL OR u.Reputation < 1000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS pct_not_high_rep FROM posts AS p LEFT JOIN users AS u ON u.Id = p.OwnerUserId WHERE p.CreaionDate >= '2010-01-01' AND p.CreaionDate < '2011-01-01' AND p.Score > 5;
answer:
33.44

Of the 2,171 posts created in 2010 with a score above 5, 726 were not made by users with reputation of at least 1000 (1,445 were). I counted the 85 posts with no owner as "not high-rep". If you would rather exclude them, the figure is 34.80% (726 of 2,086). The date column in the schema is spelled `CreaionDate`, and I used that.

sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS printing_count FROM cards AS c WHERE c.name = 'Counterspell' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM foreign_data AS f WHERE f.uuid = c.uuid AND f.language = 'French') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM foreign_data AS f WHERE f.uuid = c.uuid AND f.language = 'Italian')
answer: 9. Nine Counterspell printings have both a French and an Italian localization in foreign_data. "European" is applied only through the French and Italian condition, because the data has no European-release field. The Card and Card Foreign Data Terms are draft, not certified.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c.CustomerID) AS customer_count FROM customers AS c WHERE c.Currency = 'EUR' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM yearmonth AS y WHERE y.CustomerID = c.CustomerID AND SUBSTR(y.Date, 1, 4) = '2012' AND y.Consumption > 0) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM yearmonth AS y WHERE y.CustomerID = c.CustomerID AND SUBSTR(y.Date, 1, 4) = '2013' AND y.Consumption > 0);
answer:
1516 customers. The query returns it as `customer_count`, and I ran it read-only against `db.sqlite` to confirm the result.

Readings I chose:
- "Gas consumption" means the `Consumption` value in `yearmonth`, since that is the only consumption measure in the database. Verified query #3 also defines consumption this way.
- A month counts as having consumption only if `Consumption > 0`. The data has 28 zero values and 152 negative values, which I excluded. If zero or negative readings should count as recorded consumption, the answer would be 1517 (the count of non-null values).
- "Pays in EUR" means `customers.Currency = 'EUR'`.
- The years are calendar years, matched on `SUBSTR(Date, 1, 4)`.

sql: WITH per_event AS (SELECT b.link_to_event, SUM(x.cost) AS total FROM expense AS x JOIN budget AS b ON b.budget_id = x.link_to_budget JOIN member AS m ON m.member_id = x.link_to_member WHERE m.first_name = 'Elijah' AND m.last_name = 'Allen' AND strftime('%m', x.expense_date) IN ('09', '10') GROUP BY b.link_to_event) SELECT ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS mean_total_expense_per_event FROM per_event;
answer: Elijah Allen's mean total expense per event for expenses dated September or October 2019 is **98.77**. This comes from six events with totals of 131.77, 20.20, 295.12, 119.33, 20.20 and 6.00 (sum 592.62, divided by 6). I grouped by event ID, not event name, and filtered on the month of `expense_date`, not the event date. The query ran read-only and returned 98.77.

sql: SELECT SUM(cr.points) AS total_points, c.name, c.nationality FROM constructorResults AS cr JOIN constructors AS c ON cr.constructorId = c.constructorId JOIN races AS r ON cr.raceId = r.raceId WHERE r.name = 'Monaco Grand Prix' AND r.year BETWEEN 1980 AND 2010 GROUP BY c.constructorId, c.name, c.nationality ORDER BY total_points DESC LIMIT 1
answer: McLaren scored the most points at the Monaco Grand Prix from 1980 to 2010: 218.5 points, nationality British. Points are summed from per-race constructor results over all Monaco Grand Prix editions in that range (years inclusive). Constructor, Constructor Race Result and Race are draft Terms, not certified.

sql: WITH top_users AS (SELECT Id FROM users WHERE Reputation = (SELECT MAX(Reputation) FROM users)) SELECT ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN p.Score > 50 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS percentage FROM top_users AS t INNER JOIN posts AS p ON p.OwnerUserId = t.Id
answer:
0.66

The user with the highest reputation is user 919 (Reputation 87,393). Only one user has that value, so there is no tie. Of their 1,204 posts, 8 have a score above 50, which is 0.66%.

Reading I chose: "posts by the user" means posts where posts.OwnerUserId is that user. "Score above 50" means posts.Score > 50 (strictly greater). The percentage is 100 × count / total posts, rounded to two decimals.

The Terms used (User, Post) are still draft, not certified.

sql: SELECT l.ID, l.Date, l.RNP FROM Laboratory AS l WHERE l.GOT >= 60 AND l.RNP IS NOT NULL AND CAST(l.RNP AS REAL) = (SELECT MAX(CAST(l2.RNP AS REAL)) FROM Laboratory AS l2 WHERE l2.GOT >= 60 AND l2.RNP IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY l.ID, l.Date;
answer:
The laboratory test with the highest anti-RNP reading among tests with GOT >= 60 is patient 1650222, tested on 1989-07-18, with an anti-RNP reading of 256 (that test's GOT is 89). No other test ties at this value.

Interpretation choices: "60 or higher" is `GOT >= 60`; tests with no RNP value are excluded; RNP is compared as a number (`CAST(RNP AS REAL)`), and the reading is returned as stored. The query was run against db.sqlite and returned exactly one row.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.ID) AS patient_count FROM Patient AS p JOIN Laboratory AS l ON l.ID = p.ID WHERE p.Description IS NULL AND (l.CRP LIKE '%+' OR CAST(l.CRP AS REAL) >= 1.0)
answer:
42 patients have at least one positive CRP result and no recorded patient description.

Interpretations I chose:
- "No recorded patient description" means `Patient.Description` is NULL. In the schema, this column is the "First Data Recorded Date" (about 20% null), and the table has no separate free-text description field.
- "Positive CRP" means a CRP result that is a plus grade (`+`, `2+`, `3+`, `4+`, `5+`) or a numeric value of 1.0 or higher. This follows the ontology's note that normal CRP is `-`, `+-`, or below 1.0. Results like `<0.3` and `-` are treated as negative.

The Patient and Laboratory Terms are still draft, not certified. The result is a single row with no truncation. I did not save this as a verified example because you have not confirmed it yet.

sql: WITH seg AS (SELECT c.Segment AS segment, SUM(CASE WHEN SUBSTR(y.Date, 1, 4) = '2013' THEN y.Consumption ELSE 0 END) AS total_2013, SUM(CASE WHEN SUBSTR(y.Date, 1, 4) = '2012' THEN y.Consumption ELSE 0 END) AS total_2012 FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN yearmonth AS y ON c.CustomerID = y.CustomerID WHERE c.Currency = 'EUR' AND c.Segment IN ('SME', 'LAM', 'KAM') GROUP BY c.Segment), pct AS (SELECT segment, ROUND(100.0 * (total_2013 - total_2012) / total_2012, 2) AS increase_pct FROM seg) SELECT segment, increase_pct FROM pct WHERE increase_pct = (SELECT MAX(increase_pct) FROM pct) OR increase_pct = (SELECT MIN(increase_pct) FROM pct) ORDER BY increase_pct DESC
answer:
Highest: SME, 734.71%. Lowest: LAM, 539.83%. No ties. KAM falls between them and is not in the result.

Choices: the increase is (2013 total − 2012 total) / 2012 total × 100 on each segment's summed monthly consumption, for all EUR-paying customers in the segment. Ties were compared on the rounded values. Caveat: the data ends in November 2013, so 2013 has 11 months against 12 in 2012, which likely understates the increases. The Terms used (Customer, Monthly Customer Consumption) are draft, not certified. Percentage increase has no Term of its own, so it was built from the covered total consumption measure.

sql: SELECT r.date AS race_date, d.forename AS forename, d.surname AS surname, res.fastestLapTime AS fastest_lap_time FROM races AS r LEFT JOIN results AS res ON res.raceId = r.raceId AND (CAST(SUBSTR(res.fastestLapTime, 1, INSTR(res.fastestLapTime, ':') - 1) AS REAL) * 60 + CAST(SUBSTR(res.fastestLapTime, INSTR(res.fastestLapTime, ':') + 1) AS REAL)) > 90 LEFT JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = res.driverId WHERE r.name = 'French Grand Prix' AND r.year >= 1990 ORDER BY r.date, d.surname, d.forename;
answer:
The query returns 19 rows, one per French Grand Prix edition from 1990 to 2008 (2008 is the latest in the data), and none has a driver. No driver has a recorded fastest lap over 90 seconds in those editions, so every edition shows only its date with blank driver and lap-time fields.

Reading I chose: "fastest lap of the race" means the official `results.fastestLapTime` field, which is already in m:ss.mmm form. I compared it numerically, converting minutes and seconds to seconds, and kept only values above 90.

Two caveats:
- `fastestLapTime` is NULL for every 1990–2003 edition, so those editions cannot show a fastest lap at all. The `lapTimes` table has no rows for 1990–1995.
- In 2004–2008 the recorded fastest laps range from 1:15.377 to 1:21.663, all but none above 90 seconds (the 1:21.663 is the 2006 maximum, not a 90-second value). If you instead derive each driver's fastest lap from `lapTimes`, two 2007 drivers, Jarno Trulli (2:19.632) and Anthony Davidson (1:44.767), exceed 90 seconds. Each has only one recorded lap, a first lap ended by a collision, and no official fastest lap, so I left them out. Say if you want that reading instead.

The ORDER BY uses date, then surname, then forename. It has no visible effect here because no driver rows are returned.

sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.element = 'i' THEN a.atom_id END) AS iodine_atoms, COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.element = 's' THEN a.atom_id END) AS sulfur_atoms FROM atom AS a JOIN connected AS c ON c.atom_id = a.atom_id JOIN bond AS b ON b.bond_id = c.bond_id WHERE b.bond_type = '-' AND a.element IN ('i', 's');
answer:
Iodine: 3 distinct atoms. Sulfur: 77 distinct atoms. The query returns two columns, iodine_atoms then sulfur_atoms, in that order: 3 and 77.

Reading used: "single bond" means bond_type '-' (per the wiki and verified queries). An atom counts as participating if it appears as one end of a bond in `connected`. The sulfur count is 77 of the 94 sulfur atoms; the other 17 are not in any single bond. All 3 iodine atoms are in a single bond. I checked both counts with a separate query over the same data and they match.

sql:
WITH base AS (
  SELECT s.id, g.gender
  FROM superhero AS s
  INNER JOIN gender AS g ON g.id = s.gender_id
  WHERE g.gender IN ('Male', 'Female')
    AND s.full_name IS NOT NULL AND s.full_name <> '-'
),
power_counts AS (
  SELECT hp.hero_id, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM hero_power AS hp
  GROUP BY hp.hero_id
)
SELECT b.gender, ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(pc.n, 0)), 2) AS avg_superpowers_per_hero
FROM base AS b
LEFT JOIN power_counts AS pc ON pc.hero_id = b.id
GROUP BY b.gender
answer:
Female: 6.83, Male: 8.49 (average superpowers per hero).

Reading used: "documented real full name" means full_name is not NULL and not '-'. Each hero counts once, and heroes with no power records count as 0, so the average covers the whole gender group with a known full name. Gender and Superhero are draft (uncertified) Terms in the ontology.

"Those sets" in the base-size total is read as all sets in each block, not only the localized ones. Masques has 6 sets and Mirage has 3. Both Terms used (Card Set, Set Translation) are still draft, not certified. The query returned 2 rows, none truncated.

sql: WITH gold_accts AS (SELECT DISTINCT d.account_id, c.gender FROM card AS cd JOIN disp AS d ON cd.disp_id = d.disp_id JOIN client AS c ON c.client_id = d.client_id WHERE cd.type = 'gold'), rich_accts AS (SELECT t.account_id, AVG(t.balance) AS avg_balance FROM trans AS t GROUP BY t.account_id HAVING AVG(t.balance) > 1000), cohort AS (SELECT DISTINCT g.gender, a.district_id FROM gold_accts AS g JOIN rich_accts AS r ON r.account_id = g.account_id JOIN account AS a ON a.account_id = g.account_id), big AS (SELECT co.gender, di.district_id, di.A2 AS district_name, CAST(di.A4 AS INTEGER) AS inhabitants, di.A11 AS salary, di.A10 AS urban_ratio FROM cohort AS co JOIN district AS di ON di.district_id = co.district_id WHERE CAST(di.A4 AS INTEGER) > 100000), stats AS (SELECT gender, COUNT(*) AS district_count, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary, AVG(urban_ratio) AS avg_urban FROM big GROUP BY gender), top AS (SELECT gender, district_name, inhabitants, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY gender ORDER BY inhabitants DESC) AS rnk FROM big) SELECT s.gender, s.district_count, t.district_name, t.inhabitants, ROUND(s.avg_salary, 2) AS avg_salary, ROUND(s.avg_urban, 2) AS avg_urban_ratio FROM stats AS s JOIN top AS t ON t.gender = s.gender AND t.rnk = 1 ORDER BY s.gender, t.district_name
answer:
Women (F): 16 districts with over 100,000 inhabitants. Most inhabitants: Hl.m. Praha (1,204,953). Average salary 9245.44, average urban ratio 69.16.

Men (M): 22 districts. Most inhabitants: Hl.m. Praha (1,204,953). Average salary 9347.86, average urban ratio 71.03.

Readings chosen: gold-card holder = the client on the disposition the gold card is attached to (OWNER or DISPONENT); average balance = mean of trans.balance over all of the account's transactions; "over 100,000" is strictly greater; averages are over distinct districts. Praha is the unique largest district, so no ties. Terms used are still draft, not certified. The query returned 2 rows, not truncated.

sql: SELECT ROUND(100.0 * (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c.uuid) FROM cards AS c JOIN foreign_data AS f ON f.uuid = c.uuid WHERE (c.power IS NULL OR c.power LIKE '%*%') AND f.language = 'French') / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cards WHERE power IS NULL OR power LIKE '%*%'), 0), 2) AS french_translation_pct;
answer: 47.95%. Of the 31,078 card printings with no power value (NULL) or a variable power (contains `*`), 14,902 have a French row in `foreign_data`. I counted printings, not distinct card names, and used the same power test as verified query 4 in `docs/verified_queries.md`. The query ran and returned 47.95.
